events.text: The night before the first full moon of the year nobody in the village sleeps. You crack walnuts and chestnuts between your teeth so they will stay strong all year, you eat five-grain rice and dried greens, and the old women tell the children that whoever dozes off will wake with white eyebrows. And they tell the other thing, the one they tell every year: tonight a dragon comes down out of the sky and lays its egg in the village well, and whoever draws the first water at first cockcrow scoops up the dragon's egg, and the year's harvest with it. You are still awake when the first cock crows. From the sound of doors sliding open all down the lane, so is everybody else.

choices.text: Run. Be first at the well and float your straw on the water

ok.log: You get there first, breathless, ahead of the blacksmith's daughter by a single stride. The bucket comes up heavier than water should be. You float a twist of straw on the well to show it has been drawn, as the custom is, and carry the jar home on your head with both hands. At the bottom of it, under the cold water, lies something round, blue-green, the size of a fist, and warm.

fail.log: You are second. The blacksmith's daughter's straw is already turning slowly on the water, and the whole lane laughs at your face. But when you lower your own bucket you see, far down, a blue-green glow on the stones under the water, like a lantern behind wet paper, moving away from the light of the bucket as if it were shy.

choices.text: Let old widow Kang go first. She has never once been first

effects.log: You stop at the corner and hold the others back with your arms out like a fool, and old Kang, who has come limping down the lane every first full moon for years and never once been first, draws the first water of the year. She floats her straw with shaking fingers. Then she looks into her jar for a long moment and covers it with her skirt and does not say what she saw.

choices.text: Do not draw at all. Kneel at the rim and look down

effects.log: While the others jostle you lean over the stone rim. Under the black water, on the stones at the bottom, lies an egg, blue-green, the size of a fist, lit from inside like a lantern behind paper. As you watch, it turns, very slightly, toward you. Then the first bucket comes down and breaks the water into rings, and when the rings are gone, so is the light.

events.text: {npc}, a geomancer with a bronze compass ringed with twenty-four directions, has been hired to find you a site: a family grave, a manor, a branch hall, whatever your fortunes most need. {He} walks you through three valleys and turns back from each. The fourth has a mountain at its back, a stream winding across its mouth, and two ridges curling round it, left and right, like arms. {npc} goes very quiet. "Left azure dragon, right white tiger," {he} says. "Forty years I have read about this in books." In your sleeve is a sealed letter from a rival house: three hundred taels for nine iron stakes driven into the best ridge you find, so that no luck rises in that valley but theirs. It is the spring equinox. At dusk the left ridge rises, pines and all, the length of one slow breath, and settles. Then it lifts its head.

choices.text: Build in its embrace, and swear aloud to keep it

effects.log: You kneel on the valley floor and swear to the ridge, aloud, feeling foolish and not caring, that whatever you build here will keep it as it keeps you. The head goes down again into the pines. The wind changes and smells of new leaves, though it is barely spring. {npc} writes the date on the inside of {his} sleeve.

choices.text: Take the rival's silver and drive the nine stakes

effects.log: Nine iron stakes, each as long as a spear, driven down along the spine of the ridge with a sledge. At every blow the ground shudders under your feet, and at the seventh the whole valley sighs, and at the ninth every bird in it is gone. {npc} will not take {his} fee. The rival pays three hundred taels without a word. For a long time after, you dream of iron in your mouth.

choices.text: Bow to the ridge, and leave the valley untouched

effects.log: You bow, low, the way you would to a sleeping elder, and take {npc} by the elbow and walk out the way you came. You burn the rival's letter at the valley mouth. Behind you, as you go, the left ridge lets out its breath, and the pines all down its back stir at once as if a hand had passed over them.

events.text: Spring equinox, midnight. The seven stars of the eastern sky, Horn and Neck, Root and Room, the red Heart, the Tail and the Winnowing Basket, come down out of heaven in a line and are a dragon: azure, whiskered, long as a river, its eye the red Heart star. It coils round your courtyard with its tail out past the river, and the roof tiles ring like little bells. On the western side a white tiger the size of a hall sits down like a cat and curls its tail round its paws. "Human," the dragon says, "you are strong enough to be heard in heaven and not yet too proud to be fair. The Tiger says I took too much rain this spring." The Tiger says: "The west is dust. The east is green to the knee. Judge."

choices.text: Judge for the Tiger: the dragon took too much

effects.log: You say it plainly. The dragon's whiskers go still. For a long breath the Heart star in its eye burns very red. Then it lowers its head to the Tiger, which is the hardest thing you have ever seen a great creature do, and the next morning the west has rain. The Tiger looks back at you once as it goes, and you have the feeling a very old account has just been opened in your name.

choices.text: Judge for the Dragon: spring is the east's to give

effects.log: "Spring comes from the east," you say. "It always has. The west must wait its turn." The dragon's eye softens. The Tiger gets up without a word and goes, and where it walked the grass is white with frost. You have pleased a dragon and offended a tiger, both of them older than any kingdom, and you are not sure which will matter more.

choices.text: Judge that the rain belongs to neither: share it by the moon

ok.log: "The rain is not yours," you say to the dragon, "and the drought is not yours," to the Tiger. "It belongs to the fields. East at the waxing moon, west at the waning." There is a silence the length of a season. Then the Tiger laughs, a sound like a landslide, and the dragon laughs too, and they bow to each other across you, left and right, as if they had been waiting a thousand years for somebody small enough to say it.

fail.log: You try to split the rain between them and lose the thread halfway. The Tiger growls; the dragon's tail lashes and takes off a corner of the roof. In the end they accept your verdict, half and half, the way grown people accept a child's, and go. Your ears ring for a month. (-10 health)

events.text: Five springs after your verdict, the equinox brings visitors again, separately this time. At dusk a white tiger lies down on your western wall. At midnight a long azure shape settles along the eastern ridge with its chin on your roof. Neither speaks to the other. Both of them, plainly, have come to see you.

choices.text: Go out to the Tiger first

effects.log: You sit with the Tiger on the wall until midnight. It tells you, in a voice like gravel, what the west was like before the east was green: wheat to the horizon. It is not complaining. It is remembering. When you leave it, it puts one enormous paw on your shoulder for a moment, and your bones ache pleasantly for a week.

choices.text: Go out to the Dragon first

effects.log: You climb onto your own roof and sit by an eye as big as a cartwheel. The dragon asks you, very quietly, whether it has been proud. You tell it the truth. It thanks you for that more warmly than for the verdict.

choices.text: Ask them to sit in your courtyard together

ok.log: It takes an hour of politeness and a jar of your best wine poured out on the ground for each of them. Then they come down, left and right, and lie in your courtyard with you between them until dawn, and you understand for the first time why geomancers draw valleys the way they do.

fail.log: Neither will be the first to come down. At dawn both are gone, and you have learned that being the judge does not make you the host.

events.text: A clerk of the Eastern Palace finds you in the Upper Realm with a jade tablet. "Your verdict on the rain," {npc} says, "has been entered in the records of the Four Guardians. The Black Tortoise has read it. The Vermilion Bird has read it. The Yellow Dragon of the centre would like to know who you are."

choices.text: Go and stand before the Yellow Dragon

effects.log: The Yellow Dragon of the centre is not long or short, not old or young: it is the middle of everything, and looking at it is like standing in the exact centre of a field. It asks you only one question: "Would you judge the same again?" Whatever you answer, it nods, and the clerk writes it down.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to say you are only a passing immortal

effects.log: {npc} looks at you over the tablet. "Everybody here is passing," {he} says, "only some more slowly." But {he} writes it down. Somewhere in the Eastern Palace a long azure shape laughs in its sleep.

events.text: The egg from the well lies at the bottom of the kitchen water jar for a year. The water in that jar never goes stale, never freezes, and the rice cooked with it is so good the neighbours ask what you did. In spring the egg cracks. What climbs out onto the rim of the jar is the length of your hand, blue-green, with whiskers like threads of silk and three tiny claws on each foot. It looks at you as if it has been waiting a long time to see what you look like.
events.arc: The Thing in the Water Jar

choices.text: Tell nobody. Not one person

effects.log: You tell nobody. The old woman of the house finds out anyway, of course, and says only: "Do not tell." The little thing lives in the jar through the summer, and that year every jar in the house is full however much you draw.

choices.text: Show the village headman

effects.log: The headman comes, and his brother, and a scholar from the next village, and by evening there is a queue at your kitchen door. By morning the jar is empty and the little dragon is gone, and the water in the jar tastes, for the first time, of water.

choices.text: Feed it: grains of rice, a drop of honey, a cricket

effects.log: It ignores the rice, sniffs the honey, eats the cricket with enormous dignity, and then, while you watch, drinks a sunbeam off the surface of the water. After that you stop guessing and just leave the shutter open in the mornings.

events.text: Drought. The village children have been put in blue jackets by the headman and sent out with jars to catch lizards, for the rain rite: they will beat the jars with sticks and sing until the lizards' great cousin in the sky sends rain. A boy in blue is standing at your kitchen door, looking past you at the water jar. He has heard something.
events.arc: The Thing in the Water Jar

choices.text: Bar the door

ok.log: You stand in the doorway like a gatepost until the boy goes away. That night it rains anyway, over your house first, and then outward. The little thing in the jar is curled tight at the bottom, very pleased with itself.

fail.log: He ducks under your arm and gets a hand in the jar and is bitten, hard, by something he cannot see. He runs off howling that your jar is cursed. Nobody in the lane will draw water near your house for a year. (-6 health)

choices.text: Give the boy an ordinary lizard you catch yourself

effects.log: It takes you all afternoon behind the woodpile. The boy takes it gravely and carries it off to be sung at. That night the jar in your kitchen overflows, quietly, as if something in it were trying not to laugh.

choices.text: Take the little dragon down to the stream yourself, tonight

effects.log: You carry the jar to the stream under the dark of the moon and tip it out. It hangs in the shallows for a moment, small and blue, looking back at you. Then it is gone into the paddies, and the next morning the clouds come over the hills like oxen coming home.

events.text: Years later, at the edge of your home village, a farmer is shouting that a dog is in his paddy. It is not a dog. It is blue-green and long as a dog, with whiskers, wading through the young rice, and where it has walked the rice stands a hand taller than anywhere else. It stops. It looks at you across the paddy. It remembers the jar.
events.arc: The Thing in the Water Jar

choices.text: Wade out to it

effects.log: The water is warm as a bath around it. It puts its head under your hand like a dog, which it is not, and you stand together in the rice until the farmer stops shouting and starts staring. That autumn his paddy gives a harvest he talks about until he dies.

choices.text: Call the farmer off and say nothing

effects.log: "Only a water dog," you tell him. "Leave it be and your rice will thank you." He grumbles. His rice does thank him. The thing in the paddy watches you go, and you feel it watching all the way to the road.

events.text: The year after you let old widow Kang draw the first water, her one dry field, the stony one at the top of the village that has never fed anyone, gives the best rice in the county. She comes to your door with a sack of it on her back. "You let me be first," she says. "I saw what was in my jar. I put it back in the well before anybody woke. Was that right?"

choices.text: Tell her it was right

effects.log: She nods, satisfied, and makes you take the rice. It cooks up sweeter than any rice you have eaten, and every grain is faintly, impossibly, green at the heart.

choices.text: Ask her what it looked like

effects.log: "Like a bead of spring," she says, "with somebody inside it, looking out." She thinks. "It was not afraid of me. Nobody has not been afraid of me since I was married." She laughs, a cracked, delighted sound.

events.text: Old Kang is dying, very old, in a house that is not poor any more. She has asked for you. "Every first full moon since," she whispers, "I go to the well and something blue comes up and looks at me. It is bigger every year. Last year it was as long as a dog. You go this year. Tell it I was grateful."

choices.text: Go to the well at first cockcrow and tell it

effects.log: You are first at the well, for once, because you are not drawing water. Something long and blue rises in the black water until its eye is at the surface, and you say the words. It sinks. When you get back, old Kang has died smiling, and there is a single blue-green scale on her pillow, wet.

choices.text: Stay with her through the night instead

effects.log: She dies holding your sleeve before dawn. At first cockcrow the well in the square overflows, once, a long silver sheet of water across the stones, and stops. The whole village sees it. Nobody says what it means. Everybody knows.

events.text: Since the morning you looked down the well instead of drawing, you dream of it: the egg on the stones, lit from inside, turning toward you. Tonight in the dream it cracks, and something looks out at you, and says, in a voice like water running under ice: "You looked. Nobody else looked. They only drew."

choices.text: Ask it what it is

effects.log: "The east," it says. "Spring. A dragon, I think. I am new." It sounds pleased with all three answers. You wake with the taste of cold well water in your mouth and green shoots, absurdly, in the cracks of the floor by your mat.

choices.text: Tell it to hide from the others

effects.log: "I am a dragon," it says, a little offended. Then, after a pause: "All right." From that year on, nobody in the village ever sees the thing in the well but you.

events.text: A long time after the dream, you are walking in the hills above your old village and the whole left-hand ridge of the valley turns its head to look at you. Pines slide on its back like hair. An eye opens in the side of the hill, gold and green, wide as a pond, and you know the look in it. It is the look of something that was once looked at, and has never forgotten.

choices.text: Look back, the way you did at the well

effects.log: You stand and look, and it looks, for as long as it takes the sun to move a hand-span. Neither of you does anything else. When you go down the hill you find your step is lighter and your qi heavier, the way a river is heavier than a stream.

choices.text: Bow, and say thank you for the dream

effects.log: The eye closes slowly. The ridge settles. That night the dream comes one last time, and the voice says only: "You are welcome. Come back when you are old. I will still be here." It is, you find, a great comfort.

events.text: The blacksmith's daughter who beat you to the well that first full moon has had a strange year: her bellows never fail, her iron never cracks, and her father's forge has the best luck in the county. Now she has come to find you. "The egg," she says. "I never saw it. You did. You were looking down while I was running. Is it still there?"

choices.text: Take her to the well at night and look together

effects.log: You lie side by side on the cold rim of the well like children. Far down, after a long time, something blue turns over once in the dark. She grips your arm so hard it bruises. "Second," she whispers, "is not so bad, then."

choices.text: Tell her the first water was hers fairly

effects.log: She looks relieved and annoyed at once. "Next year," she says, "I am going to look down first." You believe her. You suspect the well does too.

events.text: The house in the dragon's embrace is built. The first winter, no snow lies on the left-hand ridge: it melts as it falls, and the pines there are green when every other tree in the province is black. {npc}, the old geomancer, comes to inspect the work. {He} puts a hand flat on the ridge and takes it away quickly, as if from a stove. "Warm," {he} says. "You swore to keep it. Now find out what that means."

choices.text: Forbid anybody to cut a tree on the ridge

effects.log: Your steward thinks you have gone soft in the head. Your woodcutters grumble. Within three years the pines on the ridge are the tallest in the province and the spring under them has never run so clear, and the grumbling stops.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to teach you to read the ridge

effects.log: All winter {npc} walks you along it: where the vein runs, where it pools, where it is tired. By spring you can feel it, faintly, under your feet, a slow pulse like a sleeper's. You never stop feeling it after that.

events.text: Strangers on the ridge above your house: three of them, in plain grey, with a sledge and a bundle of iron stakes each as long as a spear. They are measuring. You swore to keep it.

choices.text: Drive them off the ridge

ok.log: They fight like people who are paid by the stake and not by the fight. They leave the iron behind. You throw it in the river one stake at a time, and the ridge under your feet goes warm, all along its length, like a cat in the sun.

fail.log: One of them is far better than a hired hand should be. You are thrown down the slope. But they have had to fight for it, and in the morning the stakes are lying pulled out on the ridge, bent, as if something had shrugged them off. (-18 health)

choices.text: Follow them home to see who paid them

effects.log: Three days' walk behind them, to a hall with no sign on its gate and a courtyard full of iron. The vein-cutters, the old people call them. You know their gate now. They do not know your face.

events.text: Years since you drove the nine stakes. The valley below the ridge is dying: the stream has sunk into its bed, the pines have gone brown from the top down, and the families who lived there are loading their carts. Your rival house has prospered beyond anyone's dreams. You have not slept a whole night since.

choices.text: Go back with a sledge and pull the stakes

ok.log: It takes four days. The iron comes out of the ridge dark and wet, as if from a wound, and the last one is warm. That night it rains on the valley for the first time in three years. Under you, the ridge breathes out.

fail.log: You get five out before your hands are raw and your back gives. The other four you leave, for now. The stream comes back as a trickle. It is something. (-15 health)

choices.text: Tell yourself it was only business

effects.log: The rival sends you fifty taels at the new year, "for old friendship". You spend it. The dreams of iron in your mouth do not stop.

events.text: A hall with no sign on its gate sends you an invitation sealed in iron-grey wax. "You drove nine stakes into a living dragon and did not flinch," the letter says. "We are the people who do that for a living. Come and be one of our founders."

choices.text: Accept

effects.log: A hundred and twenty taels and a seat in a hall full of maps of other people's luck. You are very good at it. Somewhere, a long time from now, a dragon will know your name and the name of this hall, and will not have forgiven either.

choices.text: Refuse, and burn the letter

effects.log: You burn it in the courtyard. The ash comes down grey as iron. You go to the ridge that night and kneel there and do not know what to say, and say it anyway.

choices.text: Accept, to learn where their stakes go

effects.log: For a year you sit in their hall and memorise their maps. Then one night you are gone, and so are the maps, and in seven valleys at once the stakes come out of the ground.

events.text: Years after you bowed and left the valley of the breathing ridge untouched, you pass its mouth again. Nobody has built there. The azaleas have taken the whole valley floor, pink to the knees. And on a flat rock at the stream, where you stood that dusk, somebody has left a bowl of clear water and a sprig of pine.

choices.text: Drink the water

effects.log: It is cold as the bottom of a well in the middle of summer. Your old wounds stop aching, all of them, for a year. Up on the ridge, the pines stir in no wind.

choices.text: Leave a bowl of your own beside it

effects.log: Two bowls on the rock. You walk on. That night you dream of a valley that nobody ever builds in, and of something long that lies along its edge, keeping it, glad.

events.text: {npc}, the geomancer who took you to the valley of the breathing ridge, is very old and sends for you. "Every geomancer in the country has heard of that valley now," {he} says. "Nobody can find it. They walk round and round and come out at the same mouth. I think it is hiding. I think it is hiding because of you."

choices.text: Promise never to tell anyone the way

effects.log: {npc} smiles and burns {his} own map of it in the brazier. "Good," {he} says. "Then two of us have left it alone." {He} dies in the spring, and the valley stays hidden.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the books said would happen next

effects.log: "The books say," {npc} says slowly, "that a ridge nobody builds on and nobody cuts becomes a vein of the whole country, and that the country does not know why its springs come early." {He} closes {his} eyes. "I would have liked to see that."

events.text: On a winter night by the brazier the old woman of the house tells you, for the first time, about your mother's dream before you were born: a blue-green dragon came down out of a clear sky, coiled three times round the roof-beam, and put its head in her lap. "A dragon dream," the old woman says, "is a heavy thing for a child to carry. Do not go boasting about it."

choices.text: Promise not to boast

effects.log: You keep the promise for almost a whole month, which is longer than anybody expected. When you do tell, it is to one friend, in a whisper, behind the woodpile, and it feels like giving away something warm.

choices.text: Ask what the dragon wanted

effects.log: "Nobody knows what a dragon wants," the old woman says. "That is what makes it a dragon." She pokes the coals. "But it put its head down. It did not bite. Remember that."

choices.text: Run and tell the whole lane

effects.log: By supper the whole lane knows you are a dragon child. By the next day the boys have decided this means you must be beaten at wrestling to see if it is true. It is a long winter.

events.text: Grown, you are passing an east-facing hillside when the wind turns warm and smells of rain on new leaves, and for a moment you remember the story of the dream before you were born so clearly you could swear you were there: the roof-beam, the coil, the head put down. The ridge above you is shaped, exactly, like the dragon in the story.

choices.text: Climb the ridge

effects.log: At the top, a spring you have never heard of comes out of the rock into a basin worn smooth, and the water is warm. You sit with your feet in it until dark and come down feeling as if you had been given something you had been owed since before you were born.

choices.text: Bow to it from the road and go on

effects.log: You bow. The wind drops. Something you have carried since childhood, a small heavy thing, settles into place. You go on lighter.

events.text: Fifty days without rain. The village has given up waiting and built a dragon of its own: plaited rice straw, thick as a rice barrel and as long as the lane, with a gourd for a head and two lamp-wicks for whiskers. The plan is to drag it through the dry paddies and beat it with sticks until its great cousin in the sky is ashamed enough to rain. Nobody is allowed to fan themselves or carry a parasol, because that insults the sky. It is very hot.

choices.text: Take a stick and beat the straw dragon with the rest

effects.log: You beat it all down the lane and back. It is the best afternoon of the summer: the drums, the shouting, the dust, an old man beating the straw head with real tears on his face. At sunset one small cloud comes and stands over the village and looks at it all. It does not rain. But it looks.

choices.text: Carry water to the people pulling it instead

effects.log: Back and forth to the last well all afternoon with two buckets on a yoke. Nobody thanks you. At the end of the day the old headman drinks from your bucket and, without meaning to, says "Ah," the way you would to rain.

choices.text: Quietly sneak a fan out of your sleeve

effects.log: Three breaths of cool air and then a grandmother sees it and the whole lane turns round. You are made to carry the straw dragon's tail for the rest of the day, which is the dustiest end.

events.text: Still no rain. The magistrate has come out from the county seat. In front of the whole village, in the east hall of his office, he takes off his official hat, kneels at the great central pillar that the old people call the Heavenly Pillar, and knocks his forehead against it, again and again, until it bleeds. "If heaven is angry," he says, "it is angry at whoever governs here. Let it take it out on me."

choices.text: Kneel beside him

effects.log: You do not knock your head. You just kneel. After a while the headman kneels too, and then the blacksmith, and then the whole village is kneeling in the dust of the magistrate's yard. That night, at last, it rains: softly, from the east, the kind of rain that comes in at the window and smells green.

choices.text: Ask him whether there has been an unjust death in the county

ok.log: He looks up, blood in his eyebrows, and goes very still. There was a case: a servant hanged for a theft she did not do. He reopens it that week, clears her name, and sets up a red gate at her grave. It rains the night the gate goes up. Nobody in the county ever forgets.

fail.log: "Every county has its dead," he says tiredly, and goes back to the pillar. It rains three days later. You never find out whether it was his forehead or your question or nothing at all.

events.text: After the straw dragon summer, the straw dragon itself was coiled up and laid on the roof of the village shrine to dry out, gourd head and all. Years later it is still there, grey with weather, and children are dared to touch it. Today the roof of the shrine is wet, and only the roof of the shrine, under a clear sky.

choices.text: Climb up and look

effects.log: The old straw is soaked through and warm, and coiled in among it, just for a moment before it slips away down the eaves, is something blue-green and long as your forearm, which had plainly come to see its likeness. It looked, you think, rather flattered.

choices.text: Tell the children to leave the old thing in peace

effects.log: They leave it, grumbling. That autumn the shrine roof grows a green crop of rice from the old straw, and the whole village comes to stare at it, and the children are very smug about having left it alone.

events.text: Drought, and the county office is holding the lizard rite: a row of children in blue robes, each with a clay jar with a lizard in it, are to beat the jars with sticks and chant that they will let the lizards go when the clouds come and the rain falls. The lizards are the dragon's little kin, the clerk explains; torment them and the great one will relent. You have been given a blue robe, a jar and a stick.

choices.text: Beat the jar and chant with the others

effects.log: All afternoon in the sun. The clay rings, the chant goes round and round, and inside your jar something small scrabbles and then goes still. When it is over you open the jar. The lizard is alive, and looks at you with an expression you will remember for a long time.

choices.text: Only pretend to beat it: tap the ground beside the jar

effects.log: You hit the dust next to the jar with great enthusiasm and none of it touches the clay. The clerk does not notice. The lizard, inside, does. When you let it go at sunset, it stops on the edge of the courtyard and looks back at you before it goes into the stones.

choices.text: Let your lizard go at once and run

effects.log: You are caught, of course, and stand in the sun for an hour as punishment. But the lizard is gone, and at sunset a cloud like a long blue thread lies along the eastern hills, and does not move until dark.

events.text: Years after the lizard rite, a drought again, and the county office is choosing children in blue robes again. One small child in the row is crying, holding a jar to the chest and refusing to hit it. The clerk is raising a stick.

choices.text: Step in and take the child's place

effects.log: You put on a robe that is much too small and stand in the row of children, and the clerk is so confused he lets you. You tap the ground beside your jar all afternoon. The crying child, beside you, starts to laugh. It rains that night, from the east, gently, as if apologising for something.

choices.text: Speak to the clerk about the old rule

ok.log: "The rite asks for the dragon's pity," you tell him. "Beating a weeping child is a strange way to get it." The clerk thinks about this for so long that the sun moves, and then sends the child home. The rite goes on. The rain comes anyway.

fail.log: He tells you to mind the business of grown people. The child beats the jar, weeping. That night there is thunder but no rain, as if something had come to look and gone away disgusted.

events.text: A lizard on your windowsill this spring, every morning, in the sun. Blue-green. It does not run when you come close. On the seventh morning it is not a lizard: it is the same shape, but as long as your arm, with whiskers, and it is looking at you in exactly the way a lizard in a clay jar once looked at you.

choices.text: Hold out your hand

effects.log: It sniffs your fingers, the way you sniff an old letter, and then is gone over the roof. The jar you once held in the lizard rite is in the storeroom still. That evening it is full of clean water, though nobody filled it.

choices.text: Say sorry, out loud

effects.log: You do not know what for, exactly. It seems to. It goes, and that summer every lizard in the county sits on warm stones in the sun and nobody, child or clerk, can bring themselves to catch one.

events.text: First full moon. The village has built the moon-house on the river flat: a great cone of pine branches and straw with a little door facing east so the moon can walk in. Everyone has tied their wishes to it on strips of paper. When the moon comes up over the eastern hills, the oldest man sets it alight, the gongs start, and the sparks go up in a column. And then the column bends, and turns, and for one moment the sparks are a long whiskered shape going east.

choices.text: Shout and point, so everyone sees

effects.log: Half the village sees it and half does not and the two halves argue about it until dawn. Everybody agrees, though, that it is going to be a good year. It is.

choices.text: Watch in silence and make your wish again, quickly

effects.log: You wish the same thing again, very fast, at the long shape in the sparks. You never tell anyone what it was. Within the year, in a sideways way you did not expect, it comes true.

choices.text: Jump the dying embers with the young people, for luck

ok.log: Over and back and over, the embers hot on your soles, the gongs going. On the last jump you land and the ground under you is warm in a long line running east, and does not cool till morning.

fail.log: Your sleeve catches. Somebody puts you out with a bucket of river water, to great applause. (-6 health)

events.text: Morning after the first full moon. The children are going round calling each other's names, and whoever answers "yes" has bought the caller's summer heat. A little child calls your name across the lane. You know the trick. You also know that a dragon is supposed to have come down to the well last night.

choices.text: Answer "yes" and take the child's heat

effects.log: "My heat is yours!" the child shrieks, and runs off delighted. That summer is the hottest in years, for everyone but that child, and, oddly, you: wherever you go there is a cool wind from the east, like breath from a well.

choices.text: Stay silent and call the child's name back

effects.log: The child, outraged, answers before thinking. You have sold your heat to a five-year-old. You feel, briefly, like a great master of strategy. The child does not speak to you until autumn.

events.text: Night watch on the paddy dykes, which is the job they give the newest guard. At the third watch something wades through the young rice toward you, slow and careful: the size of a dog, blue-green, whiskered, and wherever it puts its feet the rice stands up a little straighter. It stops when it sees your spear. It does not look afraid. It looks curious.

choices.text: Lower the spear and sit still

effects.log: It comes up onto the dyke and sniffs your sandals, and then your spear, and then sits beside you like a dog that is not a dog. You watch the paddies together until the cocks crow. In the morning the rice in your section is a hand taller than anybody else's.

choices.text: Run and wake the village

effects.log: By the time you get back with torches and half the village, there is nothing in the paddy but a long smooth furrow through the rice. They laugh at you for a year. The rice along that furrow grows twice as tall.

choices.text: Thrust the spear at it: it is in the crops

ok.log: The point skids off a scale like hail off a roof tile. It looks at you, hurt and surprised, and goes into the dark. That season your section of the dyke floods twice, and only your section.

fail.log: You slip on the dyke and go into the paddy face first. When you come up, spluttering, it is sitting where you stood, looking down at you with enormous patience. (-8 health)

events.text: The thing in the paddy comes back to your dyke every few nights all summer. Now the village headman has heard rumours and offered ten taels to whoever catches "the water dog that is stealing the rice's luck". Some of the young guards are sharpening hooks.

choices.text: Warn it off: bang your spear on the dyke till it goes

effects.log: You make so much noise that the headman thinks bandits are coming. It goes. The hooks come back empty. The next spring the creek above the village runs a little higher, and you are sure it is still near.

choices.text: Lead the hook party to the wrong paddy

ok.log: You swear you saw it in the lotus pond behind the temple. They spend three nights there being eaten by mosquitoes. You spend them on your dyke with something that is not a dog.

fail.log: One of them knows you are lying. They go to your dyke instead. They find nothing, because it is cleverer than all of you, but the headman docks your pay anyway.

events.text: Years later, after a hard winter, the county is starving and a column of grey-robed people with sledges and iron stakes is walking up into the hills above your old village. You know where they are going. You remember a thing in the paddy, which will not be dog-sized any more.

choices.text: Follow them up the hill

ok.log: You catch them at the ridge and make them a great deal of trouble. They do not drive a single stake. Under your feet, the whole hillside shivers once, like a horse shaking off flies, and at the bottom of the valley the paddies are green a month early.

fail.log: There are more of them than you can handle. They drive three stakes before you are knocked down the slope. But you slowed them, and in the night the three stakes come out of the ground on their own and roll down into the river. (-16 health)

choices.text: Run to warn the village instead

effects.log: The whole village comes up the hill with flails and rakes. The grey robes do not expect that. Neither, you suspect, did whatever is lying along the ridge listening.

events.text: The Dano festival by the river: swings in the willows, women washing their hair in iris water, and the wrestling ring in the sand with a young ox tethered beside it for the champion. You have made it to the last bout. Your opponent is a miller's son built like a barn door. In the shallows behind the crowd, unnoticed, something long and blue-green is lying with its chin on a stone, watching.

choices.text: Win by strength: lift and throw

ok.log: You get your hands in the thigh sash and lift a barn door off the ground. The crowd roars. You lead the ox home. In the shallows the long shape slides away, as if it had seen what it came to see: what strength is, and what it is for, which is mostly winning oxen.

fail.log: He lifts you instead and puts you down in the sand like a sack. You lie there looking at the sky and see, over the river, a long cloud turn its head as if amused. (-6 health)

choices.text: Win by patience: let him tire himself out

ok.log: You bend and bend and do not break until he is breathing like a bellows, and then one small twist does it. The old men nod: that is wrestling. In the shallows something blows a long string of bubbles, which you choose to take as applause.

fail.log: He is more patient than he looks. In the end you both fall at once and the judges give it to him on a technicality. He gives you the ox's first calf, next spring, out of fairness.

choices.text: Let him win: the ox would feed his family all winter

effects.log: You slip, just slightly, just enough. Nobody sees but him, and he looks at you with a face you will remember. In the shallows the long shape lifts its head, considers you for a moment, and lowers it again, as if something had been settled.

events.text: Your elder sends you to the county market for a sect errand: three measures of dragon-horn shavings for a strengthening paste. Every herbalist knows dragon horn is deer antler with a story. But the old woman at the last stall unfolds a paper and the shavings inside are blue-green, curled like wood shavings, and faintly warm, and they smell of rain on young leaves. "From the bark of the east ridge," she says. "Where it rubs. In spring."

choices.text: Buy them (12 taels)

effects.log: Twelve taels, which is more than the elder gave you. You make it up from your own purse. The paste made from them heals a training wound of the elder's that has not closed in a decade, and the elder looks at you very strangely for a week.

choices.text: Ask where exactly the ridge is

effects.log: She looks at you for a long time. "Where the trees have the bark rubbed off them as high as a house," she says. "All in a line. As if something with horns coming in had an itch." She does not say which ridge.

choices.text: Buy ordinary antler and pocket the difference

effects.log: The paste is as useless as everybody expected. The old woman watches you go. That night you dream of a long itch in the bark of a ridge and wake up scratching your forehead.

events.text: You find the ridge where the bark is rubbed off the pines as high as a house, all in a line, as if something enormous with horn buds coming in had an itch. The shavings lie in drifts at the foot of the trees, blue-green and warm. Somewhere along the ridge, something is breathing.

choices.text: Gather a few shavings and leave the rest

effects.log: A handful, wrapped in a leaf. The breathing along the ridge does not change. You get the impression that a handful was acceptable and a sack would not have been.

choices.text: Find the itch and scratch it

ok.log: There is a place on the ridge where the rock is warm and rough and moves. You put your back into it with a pine branch for an hour. The whole ridge sighs. When you come down, every itch you have had for years, in every sense, has gone.

fail.log: You scratch the wrong place. The ridge twitches. You go down the slope a great deal faster than you came up. (-10 health)

choices.text: Tell your sect about the place

effects.log: The sect sends ten disciples with sacks. They come back with nothing: no shavings, no rubbed bark, just ordinary pines on an ordinary ridge. Your elder looks at you with great disappointment. You look at the ridge with great respect.

events.text: A pot peddler with a wooden carrying frame piled higher than his head is selling water jars at the crossroads market. One of them, a plain brown one at the bottom, is full of water though the others are dry, and the water in it is moving. Something in it is the size of a lizard and blue-green. It sees you looking, and puts both front feet on the rim.

choices.text: Buy that jar (3 taels)

effects.log: Three taels for a plain jar. The peddler, who has no idea, is delighted. You carry it two days home with both hands, and the thing inside rides with its chin on the rim like a child on a cart.

choices.text: Tell the peddler what is in it

effects.log: He looks, shrieks, drops the whole frame, and runs. You help the market women pick up the pots. The brown jar is empty when you get to it, and there is a wet line across the dust going toward the river.

choices.text: Ask the thing in the jar where it came from

ok.log: It cannot talk. But it looks east, very deliberately, three times. You buy the jar for three taels you find you somehow have and walk east for nine days.

fail.log: It looks at you as if you are very slow, which you suppose you are. When you turn back from asking the peddler the price, the jar is dry.

events.text: Walking east with the jar, you reach a village with a well in its square, and a twist of old straw lying on the rim from last first-full-moon, and an old woman drawing water who stops and stares at your jar. "That is ours," she says, and then, astonished at herself: "I mean, that is the well's."

choices.text: Pour the jar into the well

effects.log: The thing in the jar goes down into the dark like a dropped ribbon. The old woman bursts into tears, and then laughs, and then makes you eat three bowls of rice cooked with the well water, which is the best rice of your life.

choices.text: Ask her what the well lost

effects.log: "A peddler came at the new year and drew water before cockcrow," she says. "Before anyone. He did not know. He took the first water away to sell in the jar." She looks at the jar. "Do not be cross with him. He was only early."

events.text: You have taken work as a guard on a great building site: a lord is raising a new palace on the east ridge above the town, and the labourers have dug the foundation pit for the main hall. This morning the pit is full of water that was not there at dusk, and in the water something long and blue-green is lying very still, looking up at the sky through the timber frame.

choices.text: Run for the master builder

effects.log: The master builder comes, and the lord's steward, and then the lord himself, who stands at the edge of the pit for a long time. The next day the plans are changed. It will not be a palace. It will be a temple, with the pond left open in the middle of its courtyard.

choices.text: Climb down to the water and look closer

ok.log: It lifts its head as you come down the ladder and lets you see it properly: the whiskers, the horn buds, three claws and a fourth just coming. Then it sinks, and the water sinks with it, and the pit is empty mud. Your hands smell of spring for a week.

fail.log: The ladder is wet and so are you, very suddenly. When you climb out the pit is empty and the whole site is laughing at you. (-8 health)

choices.text: Keep the labourers back and say nothing

effects.log: You stand at the edge with your spear crossways and tell everybody it is a spring the diggers hit. By noon it has gone. The palace is built. Five years later its main hall burns down for no reason anyone can find.

events.text: The temple that was meant to be a palace is finished, with the open pond in its courtyard. The monks have asked you, the guard who saw what was in the pit, to be the first to throw a coin into the pond for luck.

choices.text: Throw the coin

effects.log: One copper into the green water. It sinks a hand's depth and stops, hanging there, and then turns slowly over and over and goes down into a dark that is much deeper than the pond. The monks say nothing. They have the look of people who have stopped being surprised.

choices.text: Throw a handful of rice instead

effects.log: "Copper is for people," you say. The abbot laughs out loud. The rice spreads on the water and is gone in a single swirl, and the pond, the monks say afterwards, has never once since been short of water in a drought.

events.text: You have taken an apprenticeship of sorts with {npc}, a geomancer, because a martial artist who can read land never picks the wrong place for a fight. {He} has you on a spur above a valley with a bronze compass on your palm. "Mountain at the back, water in front," {he} says. "The ridge on the left is the azure dragon: it should be long, and gentle, and embrace. The one on the right is the white tiger: lower, and crouching, and it must not be higher than the dragon, or the house goes to quarrels. Tell me what you see."

choices.text: Say the dragon ridge is wrong: it is moving

ok.log: {npc} stares at you, and then at the ridge, and then sits down very suddenly on a rock. "Thirty years," {he} says, "I have been waiting for an apprentice who could see that." You both watch until dark. It moves once more, the length of a breath.

fail.log: "Ridges do not move," {npc} says, and then looks again, and is quiet for a long time. "Usually," {he} adds.

choices.text: Recite the rules back perfectly

effects.log: {npc} nods. "Good. Now forget them for a year and walk the land until it tells you the same thing." It takes you three.

choices.text: Ask why the tiger must be lower than the dragon

effects.log: "Because the tiger is the stronger," {npc} says, "and strength that is not embraced by gentleness eats the house." {He} snaps the compass shut. "That is the whole art. The rest is arithmetic."

events.text: {npc} has been hired by a great family to site their patriarch's grave, and has brought you. The family's chosen spot is on the dragon ridge of a valley, right on its spine. {npc} has gone pale. "They want me to put a coffin on the neck of a living dragon," {he} whispers, "so that their grandsons will be lords. It would work. That is the worst part."

choices.text: Tell the family the site is unlucky

ok.log: You invent, with a straight face and {npc}'s compass in your hand, a great deal of unlucky arithmetic. The family buries the patriarch on the next hill over. Their grandsons are not lords, but nobody in the valley ever sees a bad year.

fail.log: They hire another geomancer who is happy to say yes. The coffin goes in on the ridge's neck. For three years the family rises like smoke. Then the ridge turns over in its sleep.

choices.text: Let {npc} decide: it is the master's name on the site

effects.log: {npc} looks at the ridge for a long time and then lies to the family, beautifully, in your hearing. On the way home {he} says, "You will have to do that one day too. Do it better than me."

events.text: {npc} is dying and has left you the bronze compass. When you open the case, the needle does not point south as it should. It swings, slowly, and settles east, and stays there however you turn it.

choices.text: Follow the needle east

effects.log: Nine days east the needle starts to tremble, and on the tenth you come over a pass into a valley held in the arm of a long ridge, and the needle points straight at the ridge, and the ridge, very slowly, opens an eye.

choices.text: Bury the compass with {npc}

effects.log: You put it in the coffin, on the old geomancer's chest. At the burial the needle can be heard through the wood, ticking east. Nobody says anything. Everybody looks east.

events.text: The elder who raised you has died, and as the strongest of the family it falls to you to choose the grave. The clan has found a site the geomancers are fighting to praise: on the inner slope of a valley, cupped in the embrace of a long pine ridge on the left. "The dragon holds the grave," the clan's old aunt says, "and the grave holds the family." Standing on it, you feel the ground under your feet rise and fall, very slowly, like a sleeper.

choices.text: Bury the elder here, in the dragon's embrace

effects.log: The bier goes up the slope with its paper flowers bobbing, the mourners wailing in hemp. When the earth is closed, the ridge above sighs, a long low sound like wind in pines, though there is no wind. In the years after, your clan does remarkably well, and nobody can say quite why.

choices.text: Choose a humbler slope across the valley

effects.log: The old aunt is scandalised and does not speak to you for a year. You bury the elder facing the dragon ridge, not in it, like a guest who knows where to sit. Somehow it feels more polite. The ridge seems to agree.

choices.text: Ask the ridge, aloud, for permission

ok.log: You stand on the slope and ask, in front of the whole clan, feeling ridiculous. After a long breath a single pine cone rolls down the slope and stops at your feet. The old aunt picks it up, bursts into tears and says that is a yes if she ever saw one.

fail.log: Nothing answers. You bury the elder across the valley, to be safe, and the clan argues about it for a generation.

events.text: Years since the burial in the dragon's embrace. Your clan has risen: two magistrates, a sect elder, a granary that never empties. And now a rival clan has started a rumour that your grave is "stealing the valley's luck" and plans to dig it up by night and pour quicklime in, which, in the old stories, kills a site.

choices.text: Guard the grave yourself, all night

ok.log: They come at the third watch with shovels and sacks of lime. They leave at the fourth without them. Behind you, the whole time, the ridge was awake: you could hear it breathing, slow and very interested.

fail.log: They are many and you are tired. A shovel catches you behind the ear. When you come round they are running, all of them, and the sacks of lime are burst and soaked through, and the ground under the grave is wet in a long line from the ridge. (-14 health)

choices.text: Go to the rival clan and share the luck

effects.log: You offer them a granary's worth of rice and a marriage between the clans. They are so astonished they accept. The rumour stops. The ridge, you think, would rather have two families to hold than one to fight over.

events.text: You are old enough now to be thinking about your own grave. You walk up to the elder's resting place in the dragon's embrace. Somebody has been keeping it: the grass cut, the stone wiped clean. Lying across the grave mound, in the spring sun, is a single long blue-green scale the size of a gate.

choices.text: Ask to be buried beside the elder

effects.log: You say it aloud to the ridge. The scale stirs in a breeze and turns over, once, which you take to be a yes. You make the arrangements that week, and feel, for the first time in years, entirely unafraid of dying.

choices.text: Ask to be buried somewhere else, to leave room

effects.log: "Others will need the embrace more than me," you tell the ridge. The scale is gone the next morning. In its place, pushing up through the grass beside the elder's grave, is a small green pine.

events.text: Meditating on a ridge at night, you hear a voice. Not in your ears: in your bones, coming up through the rock you are sitting on. "There is iron in my back," it says, very slow and very tired. "Three spans to your left. It has been there for sixty years. I would be grateful." Three spans to your left, half hidden in pine needles, the rusted head of an iron stake sticks out of the ground.

choices.text: Pull it out

ok.log: It comes out the length of a spear, black, and wet with something that is not water and glows faintly blue in the dark. The ridge under you lets out a breath that goes on for a long time. "Thank you," the voice says. "There are eight more."

fail.log: It moves a finger's width and your hands tear open on the rust. The voice says, gently, "Rest. Again tomorrow." It takes you three nights. (-10 health)

choices.text: Pull it out with qi, not muscle

ok.log: You put your palm on the iron and push your qi down along it into the ridge, and the ridge pushes back, and between you the stake slides out like a splinter from a thumb. "Clever," the voice says. "There are eight more."

fail.log: The iron drinks your qi like a sponge and gives back cold. You fall over. The voice says, "Not like that." (-12 health)

choices.text: Ask who put it there

effects.log: "Men in grey," the voice says. "With maps of other people's luck. They are paid by whoever wants the valley poor." A long pause. "They are still about."

events.text: Eight more stakes, the ridge said. You have been coming back for them, one a season, and now you have pulled five. Tonight there are people on the ridge before you: grey-robed, carrying a new stake, and a sledge.

choices.text: Fight them for the ridge

ok.log: It is a short fight in the dark among the pines. They go down the far side of the ridge carrying each other. You pull the last three stakes that same night, and when the last is out the whole ridge rolls under you, once, like a horse getting up, and lies down again whole.

fail.log: One of them hits you across the back with the sledge. As you go down, the ridge throws them, all of them, off its back and down the slope in a rattle of stones. You crawl home. (-20 health)

choices.text: Talk to them: who is paying?

ok.log: The youngest one tells you, sulkily, the name of a merchant house in the county town that wants the valley's land cheap. You go there the next week. The merchant house becomes, very quickly, much more interested in other valleys.

fail.log: They do not want to talk. One of them throws the sledge at you. You leave, and come back the next night, and the new stake is already in. (-8 health)

events.text: The ridge you cleared of iron sends for you, in its way: a dream, three nights running, of a valley green to the knees. When you go, the voice in the rock says: "I owe you. I do not like owing. Ask."

choices.text: Ask for nothing

effects.log: "Then I will remember you instead," it says, which turns out to be a great deal more than nothing. Wherever you go after that, in any valley, the left-hand ridge is a little warmer under your feet.

choices.text: Ask for strength

effects.log: It breathes once, and something comes up through the rock into your spine, slow and green and enormous, like sap rising. You come down the ridge stronger than you went up it, and taller by a finger, which nobody believes.

choices.text: Ask it what it is

effects.log: "A dragon," it says, "who lay down to keep a valley and forgot to get up. One day I will. Not yet." It sounds content. You sit with it until dawn, two patient things.

events.text: Somebody from a hall with no sign on its gate offers you a commission. {npc} unrolls a map of a far valley on the inn table: a ridge drawn as a long spine, with nine black dots along it. "We cut veins," {npc} says pleasantly. "Iron stakes, nine, at the points marked. A rich house wants that valley poor. The ridge may object. That is why we need a fighter of your quality."

choices.text: Accept the commission

effects.log: Eighty taels in advance, in iron-grey purses. {npc} shakes your hand. Theirs is very cold, as if {he} had been holding iron for years.

choices.text: Refuse, and remember the map

effects.log: You refuse politely and memorise the valley, the ridge, and the nine black dots. {npc} rolls up the map and smiles. "Someone else will say yes," {he} says. "They always do."

choices.text: Accept, and warn the valley

effects.log: You take the silver. You send a letter to the valley by the fastest courier you can buy. {npc} watches you seal it from across the inn, and does not ask.

events.text: The valley on the map. {npc} and six grey-robed cutters lay out nine stakes along the ridge at dusk. The first goes in. The ridge shivers. At the second a farmer comes running up the slope with an ox-goad and stops dead at the sight of your sword: terrified, and also, quite clearly, hiding something in a water bowl behind one hip.

choices.text: Turn on the cutters

ok.log: You put {npc} down first. The rest scatter down the slope. The farmer, still holding the bowl, sits down in the grass and laughs and laughs. In the bowl, when the farmer shows you, is a little curl of blue water that is looking at you.

fail.log: They are better than they look. You are carried off the ridge by the farmer and an ox. But only two stakes went in, and the next morning both are lying on the grass, pushed out. (-25 health)

choices.text: Let the farmer pass and pretend you saw nothing

effects.log: The farmer goes by with the bowl. You hear the farmer tell {npc}, quite steadily, that the spring they are looking for dried up years ago. {npc} believes it. The cutters drive their stakes into a dead ridge, and the living spring rides away in a farmer's water bowl under the ox's packsaddle, as it did in the old story.

choices.text: Do the job you were paid for

effects.log: Nine stakes. The ridge goes still. The farmer drops the bowl and the water in it runs away into the grass and is gone. {npc} pays you the rest. On the road home your sword rusts in its sheath, overnight, all at once.

events.text: The hall with no sign on its gate. You have found it. Inside, maps of a hundred valleys, pinned with iron nails; bundles of stakes like firewood; and a founder's tablet on the altar with a name you half recognise from a life you do not remember. The night guard is asleep.

choices.text: Burn the maps

ok.log: They go up like dry leaves. By morning the hall is ash and a hundred valleys do not know they have been saved. You watch the smoke go east, and the smoke, for a moment, is the shape of something long.

fail.log: The guard wakes. You get out with half the maps burned and a cut across your ribs. Half is not nothing. Fifty valleys sleep easy. (-15 health)

choices.text: Steal the maps and pull the stakes yourself, valley by valley

effects.log: It will take you the rest of your life. You start the next morning. In every valley you clear, somebody leaves a bowl of water on a rock for you.

events.text: You are stuck. A decision you cannot make: whether to take revenge on someone who wronged you badly, years ago, and who is now old and has grandchildren. That night, in a dream, a voice speaks to you out of a dark full of stars, and in the middle of the voice there is a red star burning like a coal. "I have a fire in my chest," it says, "that burns those who only feel. Tell me what you think, not what you feel."
events.arc: The Voice with a Fire Star

choices.text: Say what you think: revenge would feed nobody

effects.log: The red star dims a little, as if pleased, and the dream goes quiet and green. In the morning the thing you could not decide is decided, and the knot you have carried for years has untied itself in the night.

choices.text: Say what you feel, because it is the truth

effects.log: The red star flares and you wake with your chest burning as if you had swallowed a coal. It passes. Under it, when it has gone, you find that what you feel is less than you thought, and older, and tired. (-6 health)

choices.text: Ask the voice what it would do

effects.log: "I am a dragon," it says. "I would rain on them both, and let the rice decide." You wake laughing, which you have not done in a month.

events.text: The voice with the fire star comes back into your dreams, uninvited, on the night before you are to sit in judgement on a man accused of killing another. "You are going to understand, tomorrow," it says, "or you are going to feel. Choose now. I will watch."
events.arc: The Voice with a Fire Star

choices.text: Hear the whole story before judging

ok.log: It takes the whole day. The dead man had sold the accused's sister. The accused is still a killer. You find a sentence that is neither mercy nor revenge, and in the dream that night the red star burns steady and warm, like a hearth.

fail.log: You listen all day and still do not understand. You say so, honestly, and ask for time. The red star in the dream that night is neither pleased nor angry. "Honest," it says. "That is the Neck star. You are working on the wrong one."

choices.text: Judge quickly and hard: a killer is a killer

effects.log: It is over by noon. That night you wake with a burn on your chest the size of a coin, red as a star, that takes a year to fade. (-8 health)

events.text: You have not dreamed of the fire star for years. Tonight, awake, standing in your courtyard, you look up at the summer sky, at the red star low in the south-east, and it looks back. "You understood," the voice says, from up there now. "Most humans only feel. I wanted to tell you. That is all."
events.arc: The Voice with a Fire Star

choices.text: Thank it

effects.log: It flickers, once, red and gold. That is all. It is enough to keep you warm through a whole winter.

choices.text: Ask if it understood you, too

effects.log: A long pause, for a star. "No," it says. "I only felt. Do not tell anyone." You promise. You never do, until now.

events.text: Your sect's elders have discovered that the long ridge behind the mountain gate is alive, and they have a plan: bind it with a talisman rope and five years of offerings, and make it the sect's guardian beast. "Other sects have tigers," the senior elder says. "We will have a dragon." They want your vote.

choices.text: Vote against binding: ask it, do not bind it

ok.log: You talk for an hour about what a bound guardian does on the day its rope is cut. The vote turns. The sect goes up the ridge with incense instead of rope. Nothing answers for a year. Then one spring the sect's well, which has always been bitter, runs sweet.

fail.log: You lose by one vote. The rope goes on. The ridge does not resist. It does not do anything at all, for years, while the sect's luck slowly turns sour around it.

choices.text: Vote for the binding

effects.log: The talisman rope goes round the ridge, nine turns, with chanting. The sect is very proud. Under the rope, very slowly, the pines begin to die.

choices.text: Abstain, and go up the ridge alone that night

effects.log: You sit on the ridge in the dark and tell it, honestly, what the elders plan. It listens. In the morning the talisman rope will not stay tied: every knot slides loose as the elders watch. They decide the ridge is unlucky and leave it alone.

events.text: Years since the sect bound the ridge behind its gate. Three of the elders who voted for it have died young. The sect's disciples fail their breakthroughs. And this spring the talisman rope round the ridge has begun to smoke.

choices.text: Cut the rope yourself, before it burns through

ok.log: The rope parts with a sound like a breath held for years. The ridge does not take revenge. It only lifts its head, once, and looks at the sect hall for a long time, and lies down again. The next spring the pines are green.

fail.log: The talismans throw you back. But you have cut it half through, and that night the rope finishes the job itself with a crack heard three valleys away. (-20 health)

choices.text: Go before the elders and confess the vote was wrong

effects.log: It costs you your seat on the council. The rope is taken off with incense and apology. The sect's luck does not come back for a long time. But it comes.

events.text: An alchemist of a powerful sect, {npc}, invites you to dinner and, over the last cup, opens a jade box lined with red silk. In it are two hollows: one shaped like a horn, one like a small round stone. "The Azure Dragon Pill," {npc} says. "A horn of the east, and the fire star from its chest. A pill to make a human a dragon. We need a hunter. The price is a share of the pill."

choices.text: Accept the hunt

effects.log: A hundred taels and a map of an eastern valley. {npc} pours you another cup and smiles with too many teeth. "It will not want to fight," {he} says. "They never do, the old ones. That is the easy part."

choices.text: Ask what the pill does to whoever eats it

ok.log: {npc} hesitates just too long. Later, in the sect's library, you find the old recipe and the line under it in a different hand: THE ONE WHO SWALLOWS IT HAS THE DRAGON'S FIRE AND NOT ITS PATIENCE. Of the three who ate it, two burned.

fail.log: "Makes you a dragon," {npc} says, and refills your cup. You do not ask again. Something in the way {he} closed the box answers for {him}.

choices.text: Refuse and leave

effects.log: {npc} bows politely. "Someone will say yes," {he} says. On the road home you buy a horse, and ride east as fast as it will go, without being sure why.

events.text: The eastern valley on the alchemist's map. The left ridge is a dragon: you see it now, the length of the valley, its back a pine forest, horns the size of old trees. It lifts its head and looks at you and does not get up. "You have come for my horn," it says, "and the star in my chest. I am old. I do not want to fight. Is there another way?"

choices.text: Fight it: you took the silver

ok.log: It does not want to fight, and so it loses. You take one horn, and do not reach for the star, and that is the only mercy you find in yourself. The valley below is dry by autumn. The alchemist is delighted. You never sleep well again.

fail.log: It does not want to fight. It does anyway.
fail.deathCause: the dragon of the east ridge, hunted for a pill

choices.text: Lie down in its shadow and tell it who sent you

effects.log: You tell it everything: the jade box, the two hollows, the alchemist's smile. It listens like an old man listening to a grandchild. When you are done it says only, "Thank you. I will be somewhere else for a while." In the morning the valley has one ridge fewer, and a new lake.

choices.text: Take a shed horn-shaving and go home: let that be the price

ok.log: It considers this, gravely, and rubs its brow against a pine until a curl of blue-green horn falls at your feet. "Tell them that is all there was," it says. You do. The alchemist is furious. The pill is never made.

fail.log: "A thief with manners is still a thief," it says, not unkindly, and shrugs you off its ridge. You go home with nothing and a sore back, which is fair. (-10 health)

events.text: {npc}, the alchemist who wanted the Azure Dragon Pill, is dying of something no physician can name: a fire in the chest that never goes out. {He} has asked for you. "I tried to make it myself," {he} whispers. "From deer horn and a red stone. I wanted to know what it was like to be patient for a thousand years. I could not wait."

choices.text: Sit with {npc} until the end

effects.npcPass: a fire in the chest no physician could name
effects.log: You sit through the night. Near dawn {npc} says, "Was it beautiful? The dragon?" You say yes. {He} dies looking pleased, as if that had been the ingredient missing all along.

choices.text: Burn the recipe in front of {npc}

effects.npcPass: a fire in the chest no physician could name
effects.log: You hold the old paper over the lamp where {npc} can see. {He} watches it curl and does not stop you. "Good," {he} says. "Somebody should have done that four hundred years ago."

events.text: On the coast road north you fall in with the escort of a new governor and the governor's spouse, Lady Suro, who is so beautiful, the guards say, that the mountain spirits come out to look. At noon she stops under a cliff and points at red azaleas growing at the very top. "Will nobody fetch me those?" Nobody moves. The cliff is a thousand feet of wet rock.

choices.text: Climb for the azaleas

ok.log: An hour of fingertips on wet stone. You come down with an armful of red azaleas and present them, and the whole escort cheers. Then you notice that an old man leading a cow has already handed her a bunch, and is singing her a song about it. Yours are bigger.

fail.log: Halfway up the rock decides against you. You come down faster than you went up. An old man leading a cow passes, climbs the cliff like a goat, and brings her the azaleas with a little song. You will never understand it. (-12 health)

choices.text: Watch the sea instead: something is following the escort

effects.log: All morning a long dark shape has kept pace with the road just outside the surf, blue-green when the light catches it. At the seaside pavilion where the escort stops for lunch, the shape stops too.

events.text: Lunch at the seaside pavilion. Without warning the sea stands up: a wave, and in it a dragon's head as big as the pavilion, and it takes Lady Suro from her cushion as gently as a hand takes a cup and goes down into the deep with her. The governor falls on the sand. The guards draw swords at the empty sea. An old man from the village pushes through the crowd: "Many mouths melt metal! Everyone! Sticks! Strike the shore and sing!"

choices.text: Grab a stick, strike the rocks and sing with the crowd

effects.log: Two hundred people beating the shore with sticks, oars, driftwood, singing the old song at the sea: give her back, give her back, or we will catch you in a net and roast you. It is ridiculous. It is the loudest thing you have ever been part of. By dusk the sea gives up: the dragon brings her back to the beach, sheepish, and her robes smell of a perfume nobody on land has ever smelled.

choices.text: Dive in after her

ok.log: You go down into green dark until your ears burst, and at the bottom there is a palace of coral and a very surprised dragon, and Lady Suro eating something sweet off a jade plate. "Oh," the dragon says. "You came down. Nobody comes down." It sends you both back up with an apology and a fair wind.

fail.log: The deep does not want you.
fail.deathCause: the East Sea, diving after a dragon's guest

choices.text: Stand on the rocks and speak to the dragon alone

ok.log: "She is lonely in the governor's house and you are lonely in the sea," you tell the waves. "That is not the same as belonging to you." The sea is quiet a long time. Then it gives her back, and for the rest of her life Lady Suro walks on that beach every evening, and something walks with her, under the surf.

fail.log: The sea does not answer you. It answers the crowd, at dusk, when two hundred people beat the shore with sticks and sing. You learn something about the weight of one voice.

events.text: Years after the day at the seaside pavilion, the fishing village has made the shore-beating a custom: every year on that day they come down with sticks and sing the old song at the sea, half joking. This year the sea sings back: a long, low, wordless note from under the waves.

choices.text: Sing the song again, properly, as you did that day

effects.log: You sing it straight and serious, and the village stops laughing and sings with you. The note from the sea rises to meet it. Afterwards the fish come into that bay so thick you can lift them out with a basket, every year on that day.

choices.text: Listen, and say nothing

effects.log: It is an apology, you think. Or a lullaby. Or both, which is the kind of thing a sea dragon would sing. You stand on the sand with your stick until the note dies away.

events.text: Becalmed in the West Sea on a merchant ship, you dream of an old man in white rising from the waves: "I am the Dragon King of this sea. Every dawn an old fox comes down from the sky dressed as a sage and sits on the rock by my palace chanting a sutra, and my head splits open with it. You are the best shot on this ship. Shoot it." At dawn there is a rock off the bow, and on it a figure in robes, chanting, with a fox's tail just visible under the hem.
events.arc: The Archer of the West Sea

choices.text: Draw and shoot

ok.log: One arrow. The chanting stops in the middle of a word and something with nine tails goes over the back of the rock into the sea, and the sea is very still, and then very happy. The wind comes up behind the ship like a hand on your back.

fail.log: Your first arrow misses. The fox looks up at you with ancient, amused eyes. Your second does not miss, but by then it has spat something at you that burns like lamp oil. The sea is grateful anyway. (-10 health)

choices.text: Refuse: a sage is a sage, whatever the tail

effects.log: You put the bow down. The chanting goes on. The ship stays becalmed for nine days, until a fishing boat tows you in, and the captain never takes you on a voyage again.

events.text: The Dragon King of the West Sea comes up beside your ship at dusk, a head like a temple roof, and with it a person you have never seen: {npc}, in robes the colour of shallow water, with eyes like the sea at noon. "My child," the Dragon King says. "You saved my head. I would give you what I have that is most precious, and this one has decided it is going with you. I did not entirely agree."
events.arc: The Archer of the West Sea

choices.text: Accept, and take {npc} home with you

effects.log: {npc} steps from the sea onto the deck without getting wet, takes your hand, and says: "One rule. Never watch me sleep." It seems a small thing. It is the only thing {npc} ever asks of you.

choices.text: Ask for the Dragon King's blessing instead

effects.log: The Dragon King laughs like surf. A pig of gold, a jade belt and a fair wind for life. {npc} looks at you for a long moment, a little hurt, a little amused, and goes back down into the water.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what {he} wants

effects.log: {npc} looks startled. Nobody under the sea has ever asked. "The land," {he} says. "Rice. Children. Someone who asks." There is a pause. "And never to be watched asleep." You agree to all of it.

events.text: Years in the house by the sea with {npc}, and the rule has held: {npc} sleeps behind a closed door, and every morning there is a little water on the floor of that room, and a smell of salt. Tonight there is a storm, and from behind the door comes a sound like waves breaking, and something long and heavy moving.
events.arc: The Archer of the West Sea

choices.text: Keep the rule: stay out

effects.log: You sit outside the door all night with your back to it, listening to the sea in the next room. In the morning {npc} opens it, tired and dry-eyed, and sees you there, and understands what you did not do. Nobody has ever looked at you like that, before or since.

choices.text: Open the door a crack

effects.log: A crack. Inside, the room is the sea, and coiled in it, filling it, is an azure dragon with {npc}'s eyes, asleep. It wakes. It sees you. Neither of you says anything. In the morning there is a well dug in the yard that was not there before, and {npc} is gone into it, and in the well, every morning afterwards, the water is warm.

events.text: A young person comes to your door with sea-coloured eyes and a scale behind one ear, blue-green, the size of a coin. "I am your grandchild," {npc} says. "By the one who went into the well. I was told to ask you one thing: should I go and be a king? Everybody says I could."
events.arc: The Archer of the West Sea

choices.text: Tell {npc} to be a king, and a humble one

effects.log: {npc} goes. Thirty years later there is a new kingdom on the west coast whose founder never sits higher than the people at a feast, and whose royal robe has a dragon on it with its head bowed.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to be a fisher, and happy

effects.log: {npc} laughs out loud, exactly the way {his} grandparent used to. "That is what the well said too," {he} says. The west coast gets no new kingdom. It does get the best fisher in its history.

events.text: The coastal command has given you a warship: a new galley with a dragon's head carved at the bow, its mouth a vent for sulphur smoke. The shipwright, {npc}, confesses that {he} did not carve the head from imagination. "It sat for me," {npc} says. "Three nights, in the harbour. It asked for one thing: that whoever commands this ship never runs from a fight that protects the shore, and never chases one that does not."

choices.text: Swear to it, on the bow

effects.log: You put your palm on the carved head and swear. The wood is warm. The galley handles, from that day, as if it knew where you wanted it before you did.

choices.text: Laugh: a ship is a ship

effects.log: {npc} does not laugh. On the galley's first voyage the dragon head will not face the wind, whatever the helmsman does, and you go back to harbour with the whole fleet watching.

events.text: Raiders off the coast, sixty sail, and your dragon-headed galley is the only warship within a day. Your officers want to fall back and wait for the fleet. The fishing villages behind you will not last a day.

choices.text: Hold the strait: the oath

ok.log: One ship against sixty. The dragon head breathes its smoke and, under your keel, the sea itself gets up and goes with you, a long swell that capsizes the raiders' front rank before your archers loose a single arrow. By dusk the strait is yours. The fishing villages hang dragon lanterns for a year.

fail.log: One ship against sixty is too many, even with the sea.
fail.deathCause: the strait, holding a dragon-headed galley against sixty raiders

choices.text: Fall back and fetch the fleet

effects.log: The fleet comes. Two villages burn before it does. On the way back, the dragon head on your bow is split down the middle, cleanly, as if it had been cut. The shipwright will not repair it.

events.text: A white tiger the size of a hall walks into your courtyard at sunset, lies down, and puts its chin on its paws. "They say you are a fair judge," it says. "I have a grievance against the Dragon of the East. For three hundred years it has taken the spring rain. My west is dust. Nobody listens to a tiger. Everyone is afraid of tigers."

choices.text: Hear the whole grievance
