effects.log: It talks until the moon is high: the wheat it remembers, the herds, the dragon growing proud and green on its ridge. It is not wrong. It is not entirely right. It is lonely, mostly, and you are the first to sit and listen.

choices.text: Ask it why it does not take the rain back by force

effects.log: "Because the valley between us would be the battlefield," it says. "And I like the people in it. They put out rice for me at the new year, as if I were a cat." It looks embarrassed. You do not laugh.

choices.text: Tell it to take its grievance to heaven

effects.log: "Heaven," the Tiger says, "is in the east." It gets up and goes, and that autumn your courtyard has frost on it every morning, and only your courtyard.

events.text: You have walked east to the Dragon's ridge to carry the Tiger's grievance. The ridge is a dragon, the length of a valley, with temples on its back and a festival in its honour going on below. It listens to you with one enormous eye half shut, the way a great lord listens to a clerk.

choices.text: Tell the dragon it has grown proud

ok.log: The eye opens fully. For a long moment you think you are about to die. Then it laughs, a sound like a landslide in spring, and says: "Nobody has told me that in two hundred years. That is how I know it is true." That year the west gets its rain.

fail.log: The eye opens. A wind comes off the ridge that knocks you flat and rolls you down the valley like a leaf. When you stop, the west is still dry. But the next spring, quietly, the rain goes there first. (-20 health)

choices.text: Propose a bargain: east at the waxing moon, west at the waning

effects.log: It thinks about it for a whole day, with the festival going on obliviously underneath. Then it says, "Tell the cat yes." You carry the answer back west, and the Tiger, when it hears, rolls over on its back in the dust like a kitten.

events.text: The old king of the eastern kingdom is dying, and has sent for you, because you are the only human in the land strong enough to be heard under the sea. "Burn me," {npc} says, "and put my ashes in the rock in the East Sea. I will become a dragon and guard the coast against raiders forever. But the Dragon of the East is already there. Ask it, for me, whether it will share."
events.arc: The King Who Wanted the Sea

choices.text: Go down into the East Sea and ask

ok.log: You go down past where light stops. The Dragon of the East is waiting, coiled round the base of the rock. "A king who wants to be a dragon," it says, amused, "and a human brave enough to ask. Tell the king yes. And to bring a good flute." You come up with blood in your ears and the answer.

fail.log: The sea does not let you get far. But at the depth where you turn back, a voice in the water says: "Yes. Tell the king yes." You come up half drowned with the answer anyway. (-20 health)

choices.text: Ask {npc} why a king would choose to be a dragon

effects.log: "Because a king dies," {npc} says, "and a coast does not stop needing guarding. And because I am afraid of the dark, and dragons are not." {He} laughs weakly. "Go and ask."

events.text: The old king's ashes are in the rock in the East Sea now, and the new king has built a temple on the shore with a stone channel under the main hall so that the sea, and whatever lives in it, can come in. Tonight a little island has floated up to the shore, with one bamboo on top: two stalks in the day, one at night.
events.arc: The King Who Wanted the Sea

choices.text: Cut the bamboo, as the dragon said

effects.log: One stroke, at the moment the two stalks become one. The island sinks with a sigh. The new king has the bamboo made into a flute, and when it is played, for the first time, the sea goes flat as a mirror from the shore to the horizon, and every sick person in the palace sits up.

choices.text: Leave it: the gift is not for you to take

effects.log: You wait on the shore until the new king comes down himself, as perhaps it was meant. You watch him cut it. Later, hearing the flute from a distance, you find you do not mind at all that it was not your hand.

events.text: Years after the flute was cut, raiders come in sixty ships toward the east coast. On the palace wall a musician is trembling with the flute at the lips. On the rock in the sea, two long shapes have risen: the old Dragon of the East, and beside it, smaller and newer, something that was a king.
events.arc: The King Who Wanted the Sea

choices.text: Stand with the musician and steady the breath

effects.log: You put your hand flat between the musician's shoulders and breathe with them. The first note goes out over the water. The sea lies down. The sixty ships sit on a flat sea with their sails hanging, and then, quietly, turn round. The two dragons on the rock watch them go.

choices.text: Go down to the shore and fight with the dragons

ok.log: There is not much fighting. The ships that reach the shore are met by you, and the two dragons, and the flute, and the sea. The raiders do not come back in your lifetime, or in the next king's.

fail.log: You fight on the beach until the flute finds its note. Then the sea does the rest. You are carried up the beach by something that was once a king, which is a story nobody believes. (-20 health)

events.text: Heaven has sent its punishment for the Dragon of the East Ridge: it gave rain without leave in a drought, to a valley heaven had decided should go dry. The sky over the ridge is black from horizon to horizon and the lightning is walking down it like a man coming down stairs. The valley's people are running. The ridge is not. A ridge cannot run.

choices.text: Stand on the ridge and hold the sky off it

ok.log: You take the first bolt on your palms. And the second. By the ninth you are on your knees and the ridge under you is so still you can feel it holding its breath. The tenth does not come. The sky thins. Somewhere very high up, somebody with a brush crosses something out.

fail.log: Heaven is heavier than you are.
fail.deathCause: heaven's lightning, standing on a dragon's ridge

choices.text: Get the valley's people out

effects.log: All night in the rain, carrying the old and the sick down the valley. Behind you the lightning falls on the ridge, again and again. In the morning the ridge is burnt black. Then, at noon, from the burnt pines, very slowly, green shoots. (-8 health)

choices.text: Petition heaven, loudly, with qi behind every word

ok.log: You stand on the highest rock and shout up into the storm about rice, and children, and the fact that the valley would have died. The storm pauses. Then, as if embarrassed, it drifts off sideways and rains itself out over the empty sea.

fail.log: A bolt comes down near enough to answer you. It knocks you into the valley. But it was the last one. (-15 health)

events.text: A clerk of heaven, {npc}, comes down to you with a scroll and an expression of great weariness. "You interfered," {he} says, "with a sentence on the Dragon of the East Ridge. Heaven would like to know why. Briefly. In writing."

choices.text: Write it: the dragon saved a valley, and the law was wrong

effects.log: You write three pages. {npc} reads them twice and rolls up the scroll. "It will be filed," {he} says. Forty years later, in a drought in the same valley, heaven sends rain on its own, early, without being asked. Someone read it.

choices.text: Refuse to write anything

effects.log: {npc} sighs. "You realise this goes on your record," {he} says. "Every life." You say that is fine. {He} writes it down. It does.

events.text: The Dragon of the East Ridge, whom you once held the sky off, comes to you as a person: old, in blue, with pine needles in the hair and a scar like a lightning bolt from brow to jaw. "You stood on my back," it says. "I have thought for a long time about what to give you. I have decided on advice."

choices.text: Ask for the advice

effects.log: "Dive in autumn," it says. "Whatever you are, rest in the dark one season a year, or you will become too bright to see by." You think about it for the rest of your life, and every autumn you take a season off, and you are never once too proud to see.

choices.text: Say it owes you nothing

effects.log: It smiles, a long slow smile like a valley in spring. "That is what I hoped," it says. "That is why I came." It is gone before you can answer, and the courtyard smells of pine.

events.text: A great drought, and the old king, {npc}, is dying in the middle of it. {He} has made every sacrifice there is: the altars, the lizard rite, the straw dragons, the bare head in the sun. Now {he} has sent for you. "When I die," {he} says, "I will go up and ask heaven myself. But I am afraid I will not be heard. You are strong enough to be heard. Go to the Dragon of the East and tell it: the day I die, let it rain."

choices.text: Go to the dragon and carry the promise

effects.npcPass: old age, in the great drought
effects.log: Three days east. The dragon hears you out with its eye half shut. "A king's promise," it says, "is a heavy thing to carry for a dead man." Then: "Tell the king yes." You ride back. The king dies on the tenth day of the fifth month, and it rains so hard that by the end of the month the rivers are over their banks.

choices.text: Promise {npc} it will rain, and stay at the bedside

effects.npcPass: old age, in the great drought
effects.log: You do not go anywhere. You hold {npc}'s hand and promise. {He} dies at noon. At one, out of a white sky, it starts to rain. You do not know, then or ever, whether you lied.

events.text: The tenth day of the fifth month, a year after the old king's death. The sky is clear. The whole capital is on its roofs, staring up. And at noon, from nowhere, it rains.

choices.text: Stand in it with your face up

effects.log: It is warm. It tastes, faintly, of ink and of pine. Around you the whole city is laughing and crying at once. They will call it the King's Rain. On that day every year after, as long as you live, it rains.

choices.text: Look east for the dragon

effects.log: Far over the eastern hills, in the rain, a long shape lies along a cloud like a sleeper along a bench, keeping a dead man's word. You bow to it. It does not see you. It does not need to.

events.text: A messenger who is a crane lands on your gate and speaks: "The Dragon of the East is to take the Eastern Seat at the spring equinox. The Four Guardians require a human witness strong enough to stand the sight. You have been named."

choices.text: Accept

effects.log: The crane bows and flies east. You spend the winter wondering what a human is supposed to wear to the crowning of a constellation.

choices.text: Ask why a human is needed

effects.log: "Because the east is where humans plant," the crane says. "Its guardian is crowned in front of somebody who eats rice. It has always been so." It looks you over. "You eat rice?" You do.

events.text: The spring equinox. On the highest peak in the east, you watch the Dragon of the East rise through the storm toward seven stars that have arranged themselves into an empty seat. Halfway up it stops, and turns its head, and looks down at you. Every witness, it seems, is asked one question. "Was I humble?"

choices.text: Answer honestly, whatever the answer is

effects.log: You tell it the truth, the good and the not so good. It listens all the way to the end. Then it goes up, and takes the seat, and the seven stars blaze, and spring comes to the east a full month early, and the first thing it does as Guardian of the East is rain, gently, on the peak where you are standing.

choices.text: Tell it that asking is the answer

effects.log: It laughs, a sound like ice breaking on a river. "A clever witness," it says. "Good. I was afraid of a flatterer." It goes up into its seat. On the east wall of every tomb painted after that year, the painters swear, the dragon's eye has a look of amusement in it.

events.text: Guarding the royal embroidery workshop for a season, you watch the old head embroiderer, {npc}, at work on the king's new robe: a golden dragon roundel on the chest, five claws. {npc} has stopped, needle in hand, and has not moved for an hour. "It came last night," {he} says, without looking up. "To see. It said the claws were wrong. Four, it said, or it is lying."

choices.text: Tell {npc} to sew four claws

effects.log: Four claws. The court is scandalised. The king, when the robe is brought, looks at it for a long time, and then at the old embroiderer, and then wears it, and in all the years the robe is worn, the king never once starts a war.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to sew five: the king wants five

effects.log: Five claws, gold on red, magnificent. The king loves it. The robe catches fire, inexplicably, at the next new year feast. Nobody is hurt. The robe is not repaired.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what else it said

effects.log: "It said," {npc} says slowly, "that a king who wears a dragon should be able to say what the dragon is guarding. And that most cannot." {He} goes back to sewing. You think about it for weeks.

events.text: A tomb painter hires you to hold the lamp in a king's burial chamber: four walls of smooth granite slabs, lime-washed, the guardian of each direction to be painted on its own wall. {npc} is grinding blue stone in a mortar for the east wall, very slowly. "Every painter paints the dragon from somebody else's painting," {he} says. "I want to paint it from the dragon. Will you come with me east, and stand guard while I look?"

choices.text: Go east with {npc}

effects.log: Nine days east to a valley with a ridge that breathes. {npc} sits on a rock in front of it for a whole month, not painting, only looking. On the last day the ridge lifts its head and looks back, and {npc} weeps, and grinds a new pigment that night with something blue in it that did not come from any stone.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to paint it from imagination

effects.log: {npc} paints it from imagination, and it is very fine, and every visitor admires it. {npc} is never satisfied, and on the last day goes back alone into the dark chamber, and comes out with blue on {his} fingers, and will not say what was changed.

events.text: The painter's east wall is finished, and the chamber is to be sealed tomorrow with the king inside. Tonight, holding the lamp for the last time, you see that the painted dragon's eye is not quite where {npc} put it. It has moved, a little, toward the coffin.

choices.text: Point it out to {npc}

effects.log: {npc} looks for a long time. "It is choosing," {he} says quietly. "It has decided to stay." The tomb is sealed at dawn. On your way out you feel the walls behind you settle, as if somebody had sat down for a very long watch.

choices.text: Say nothing, and bow to the wall

effects.log: You bow to a painting. The lamp flame leans toward it, as if in a draught, though the chamber is still. Outside the stars of the east are very bright.

events.text: Fire in the palace: the great banquet hall on its forty-eight stone pillars over the pond is burning from the roof down. You are on the bucket line from the pond, and under the black water, lit orange by the fire, something very long is moving back and forth, back and forth, like a dog behind a gate.

choices.text: Climb onto the roof with a soaked cloak

ok.log: An hour on a burning roof, beating out sparks. The hall is saved, mostly. When you climb down the pond is steaming, and the thing in it has gone still at the bottom, and you have the strange impression that it is grateful and furious at once.

fail.log: The roof goes under you and you drop through into the pond. Something catches you before you reach the bottom and pushes you up to the bank. The hall burns. You live. (-18 health)

choices.text: Kneel at the pond and speak to whatever is in it

effects.log: "Help," you say, which is the whole of your plan. The pond surges once, a wave up over the stone edge and across the burning floor. It is not enough. But in the morning, when the ashes are cold, there are wet claw marks on the stones, four toes wide, all round the ruins.

events.text: The banquet hall is being rebuilt on its pillars over the pond. The court geomancer has proposed something: two dragons cast in bronze, sunk in the pond, so that the water's power will subdue fire forever. The bronze-caster asks you, as one who was there the night of the fire, to cast the first ladle.

choices.text: Cast it, and drop the dragon in the pond yourself

effects.log: The bronze dragon goes into the green water with a heavy, satisfied sound. For a moment, under it, something longer and bluer turns over and settles round it, as if lying down beside a friend. The hall never burns again in your lifetime.

choices.text: Ask whether the thing in the pond wants company

effects.log: The caster looks at you as if you were mad. Then, slowly, as if not mad. They cast two, a little smaller than planned, with their heads turned toward each other. Nobody can say why that feels right. It does.

events.text: Spring equinox. At dawn, in the east, a single long cloud lies along the hills, and for a breath it has whiskers, and then it does not.

choices.text: Make a wish for the year

effects.log: You wish for a good harvest, which is the oldest wish there is. Somewhere, something long and green seems to have heard that one before, and not minded.

choices.text: Breathe in the east wind and meditate

effects.log: The east wind at the equinox is green and cold and full of something rising. You breathe it until the sun is up and go about the day feeling as if you, too, had just come up out of a long dark.

events.text: In the Upper Realm there is a road east that ends at seven halls in a row, each lit by one star: Horn, Neck, Root, Room, Heart, Tail, Winnowing Basket. From far off, the seven halls together are a dragon. The gatekeeper of the first, a horned youth with a spring branch, bows. "Each hall has a trial," {npc} says. "Courage, honest speech, patience, shelter, understanding, legacy, judgement. The dragon who owns them passed all seven. Would you like to try?"
events.arc: The Seven Halls of the East

choices.text: Walk the seven halls

ok.log: It takes you seven years. In the Horn Hall you go first into the dark. In the Neck Hall you tell a truth that costs you. In the Root Hall you sit still for a year. In the Heart Hall the red star burns you, and you understand why. At the end, in the Winnowing Basket, a wind blows through you and takes away a great deal of chaff you did not know you were carrying.

fail.log: You pass the Horn and the Neck and stall in the Root Hall, where the trial is to sit still, and you cannot. {npc} brings you tea every morning for a year and says nothing. You leave humbler than you came, which, {npc} says, is the Root Hall's real trial.

choices.text: Ask {npc} which hall is hardest

effects.log: "Everyone thinks it is the Heart," {npc} says. "The fire star. It is not. It is the Root Hall. Patience. Immortals are the worst at it. They have so much time they think they need none." {He} laughs at your face.

events.text: The keeper of the Horn Hall finds you again. "The dragon of the seven halls wants to meet the immortal who walked them," {npc} says. "It does not meet many. It is shy, for something the size of a constellation."
events.arc: The Seven Halls of the East

choices.text: Go and meet it

effects.log: It comes down out of its seven stars and lies along the road like a river of night, and asks you, very politely, what it is like to be human, because it has forgotten. You tell it about rice, and wells, and the first full moon. It listens with its whole length.

choices.text: Send it a gift instead: a bowl of well water from the world below

effects.log: It takes you a year to fetch. {npc} carries the bowl in. That night all seven halls are lit at once, brighter than they have been in a thousand years, and someone in the Heart Hall is heard laughing.

events.text: You are summoned to the hall of the Four Guardians: the Azure Dragon on the east side, the White Tiger on the west, the Vermilion Bird on the south, the Black Tortoise with its snake on the north, and in the centre the Yellow Dragon, who presides. The record of the Azure Dragon is being judged. "You lived below," the Yellow Dragon says. "Was it a good guardian? Testify."

choices.text: Testify to its kindness

effects.log: You tell them about wells that never ran dry and valleys that never had a bad year. The Vermilion Bird nods. The Tortoise writes. The Azure Dragon looks at the floor, embarrassed, which counts in its favour.

choices.text: Testify to its pride

effects.log: You tell them about temples on its back and festivals in its name and the way it took the spring rain. The Tiger growls agreement. The Azure Dragon does not look away from you once. When you finish, it bows to you, the deepest bow in the hall.

choices.text: Testify to both, plainly

ok.log: Kindness, and pride, side by side, without softening either. The hall is silent. The Yellow Dragon says: "That is the first testimony in three thousand years that I believe." The record is closed. The Azure Dragon keeps its seat.

fail.log: You try to say both and say neither well. The Black Tortoise sighs and writes "inconclusive". The Azure Dragon catches your eye and, very slightly, shrugs.

events.text: The White Tiger of the West finds you alone in a cloud garden of the Upper Realm. "You testified," it says. "I want to know something. Down there, in the valley between us, did the people know we were there? Either of us?"

choices.text: Tell it: they put out rice for you at the new year

effects.log: The Tiger is quiet for a long time. Then it purrs, which in a creature that size is like a millstone turning, and the whole garden shakes its blossoms down.

choices.text: Tell it: no, and that was the best of it

effects.log: "Yes," the Tiger says, slowly. "A guardian you can see is a lord. A guardian you cannot see is a mountain." It looks east, toward the Dragon. "Tell it I said so."

events.text: The Blue Emperor of the East, who was once a dragon and is now spring itself, asks for an audience with you. There is a dead world below the Upper Realm, it says: grey, frozen, no seasons. "I cannot go," the Blue Emperor says. "If I leave the east, the east forgets to bloom. You are a sovereign. You could carry a spring there."

choices.text: Carry it

effects.log: It puts a seed of green light in your hands, warm as an egg. You carry it down through the cold for a hundred years. Where you set it down in the grey, a crack appears, and in the crack, a shoot. You stay until the first rain. It takes a long time. It is worth every year.

choices.text: Ask the Blue Emperor what it was like to be a dragon

effects.log: "Long," the Blue Emperor says. "And wet. And there was a well, at the very beginning, and a human who looked down." It smiles, and the hall fills with the smell of rain on new leaves. "I think about that human more than about my whole reign."

choices.text: Decline: a sovereign has a world of their own to keep

effects.log: The Blue Emperor bows, unoffended. "That is the right answer for a sovereign," it says. "And the wrong one for a gardener." It sends someone else. You watch the dead world from far off, and see it, after a long while, turn faintly green.

events.text: The world you carried spring to is green now: rivers, rain, the first creatures in the shallows. And in a well that its first people have dug, on the first full moon of its first year, something blue-green lies on the stones under the water, the size of a fist.

choices.text: Go down and look at it

effects.log: You kneel on the rim of a well in a world you planted, and look down, and it turns, very slightly, toward you. You have the strangest feeling that the whole long story has just started again, and that this time, it knows who you are.

choices.text: Leave it for the world's own people to find

effects.log: At first cockcrow you watch from a hill as a young woman runs to the well, first of all the village, and draws, and floats a twist of grass on the water, and carries her jar home with both hands. You go back up to the Upper Realm very quietly.

events.text: In the treasury of a coastal lord, where you are a guest for the season, there is an old bamboo flute on yellow silk with a label so faded you can only read two words: TEN THOUSAND. When you walk past it, every night, it breathes: a faint sound, like the sea heard from a long way off. Tonight it is louder, and the hair on your arms stands up, because you know that sound. You were the bamboo.

choices.text: Pick it up and play one note

ok.log: One note, low and long. Outside, the sea, which has been rough for a week, lies down flat from the harbour to the horizon like a dog told to sit. Every sick person in the lord's house sleeps through the night for the first time in a month.

fail.log: No sound comes. Then, very faint, from the flute and not from your breath, a sound like waves going back down a beach. You put it back on the silk with shaking hands.

choices.text: Leave it, and ask the old steward its story

effects.log: "A king lay down in the East Sea to become a dragon," the steward says, "and the dragon of the east gave him a bamboo off its own ridge. When it is played, storms lie down and raiders turn back." The steward looks at you oddly. "It has never made a sound on its own before you came."

events.text: Raiders. Forty ships off the coast at dawn, and the lord's soldiers are not enough, and the lord himself has come down to the treasury in his nightclothes, staring at the flute on its silk. "Nobody has been able to play it for two hundred years," he says. "The guards say it plays for you."

choices.text: Take it to the harbour wall and play

effects.log: You stand on the wall with forty sails coming in and play the only tune you know, a children's song about rice. The sea flattens under the raiders like a hand pressing silk. Their sails hang. One by one, without a blow struck, they turn and row away. Behind you, the whole town is silent. Somewhere under the water, something very long is lying with its chin on the seabed, listening.

choices.text: Give the flute to the lord: it is his to play

ok.log: You put his hands on it and show him how to breathe from the belly, not the chest. It takes him three tries. On the third the sea lies down. He never forgets who taught him, and never again calls it his.

fail.log: He cannot make it sound. In the end you play it with the raiders already on the beach, and the sea takes the ships and not the men, and the fighting on the sand is ugly. (-15 health)

events.text: A fishing village on the east coast keeps a shrine to the King Under the Sea. On its altar, among the shells and coins, is a little bamboo pipe a child has carved. When you pass, the sea in the bay goes glassy, and an old fisherwoman looks up from her nets at you, then at the sea, then at you again.

choices.text: Play the child's pipe

effects.log: It squeaks horribly. The sea, which knows exactly who you are, lies flat anyway, out of courtesy. The fisherwoman laughs until she cries.

choices.text: Leave an offering and go

effects.log: A coin, a bow, a long look at the sea. As you walk away along the shore the waves follow you, very small and very polite, all the way to the headland.

events.text: Hunting bandits in the northern hills, you shelter in an old grave mound that has been robbed and left open. Inside, by torchlight, the chamber is granite slabs, and on each wall a guardian: a tiger, a bird, a tortoise with a snake. On the east wall the dragon has faded almost to nothing, thirteen hundred years of damp. Only the eye is still bright. It is looking at you. You know, with your whole body, what it felt like to be poured into that wall.

choices.text: Put your hand on the east wall

effects.log: The stone is warm under your palm. In the dark you hear, or remember, a dying king's voice: guard me. And the painter grinding blue stone. And thirteen hundred years of a sleeper's breathing in the next room. You take your hand away, and there is a little blue on your fingers.

choices.text: Seal the robbed entrance with stones

effects.log: It takes you a day and a night. When the last stone is in place, you hear from inside, very faintly, a sigh, as if somebody who had been sitting up too long had finally been allowed to lie down.

events.text: A party of court scholars has come north to copy the old tomb murals before they fade entirely. Their head scholar, {npc}, is in despair over the east wall. "There is nothing left of it," {he} says. "Only an eye. We cannot copy an eye."

choices.text: Describe the dragon to {npc}, scale by scale

ok.log: You describe it all afternoon, things nobody living could know: the curve of the neck, the three-and-then-four claws, the pearl-grey whiskers. {npc} paints it from your words with tears running down {his} face. The copy hangs in the royal library for six hundred years.

fail.log: You know it, but you cannot say it. The words come out like water through fingers. {npc} paints the eye alone, very carefully, and the copy of the east wall is the strangest painting in the royal library: a blank wall, with one eye.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to leave the east wall as it is

effects.log: "Some guardians," you say, "fade because the job is done." {npc} looks at the eye for a long while, and copies only the tiger, the bird and the tortoise, and leaves a space on the scroll where the east should be.

events.text: Every so often, all your life, you have dreamed of a dark room and a long watch. Tonight the dream is different: the sleeper in the next room has sat up. "Thirteen hundred years," says an old king's voice, cracked with dust. "You can go now. I am not afraid of the dark any more."

choices.text: Say you were glad to stay

effects.log: You wake with your face wet and your heart very light. All that year, wherever you sleep, you sleep the whole night through.

choices.text: Ask the king what the dark was like

effects.log: "Like the inside of an egg," the king says. "Warm. Blue. Someone keeping watch." A dry laugh. "I recommend it."

events.text: A sect auction in a lantern-lit hall. The last lot is brought out on black lacquer: a single pill, blue-green, the size of a lotus seed, glowing faintly. "The Azure Dragon Pill," the auctioneer says. "Horn of the east and the fire star from its chest, ground by our founder six hundred years ago. Whoever swallows it will have a dragon's power." Your chest hurts. Not a little. As if something had been taken out of it and you have only now noticed.

choices.text: Bid for it, whatever it costs (300 taels)

effects.log: Three hundred taels, and the room hates you. On the lacquer tray, as you take it, the pill goes dark and cold, as if it had been waiting for a particular hand and could stop glowing now.

choices.text: Stand up and tell them what it is made of

ok.log: You tell them: an old dragon on a ridge that did not want to fight, a horn, a heart, a valley that went dry. You do not know how you know. The room goes very quiet. No one bids. In the end the sect's elder brings the pill to you on its tray, without a word, and leaves.

fail.log: They laugh you out of the hall. The pill goes to a young master of a great family for four hundred taels. You hear, the next year, that he swallowed it and burned from the inside for a month.

choices.text: Leave the hall: you cannot breathe here

effects.log: Outside in the cold you breathe until your chest stops hurting. Through the paper doors you hear the gavel come down. You do not ask who bought it. You find you never want to know.

events.text: The Azure Dragon Pill is in a box under your bed. On spring nights it glows, faintly, and you dream of a ridge, and a valley, and iron hooks. It has taken you years to decide what to do with it.

choices.text: Swallow it

ok.log: It goes down like a coal. For a month you burn. When the fever breaks you are stronger than you have ever been, and you can hear rain coming a day away, and you never, ever, feel warm again in spring.

fail.log: The fire star in it does not want a second chest.

choices.text: Carry it east and bury it in a living ridge

effects.log: Nine days east to a valley with a ridge that breathes. You dig a hole the depth of your arm in the pine needles and put the pill in it. The ridge goes still. Then, under your knees, slowly, it starts to breathe again, a little deeper. You walk away feeling as if you had been forgiven by yourself.

choices.text: Grind it into a well

effects.log: You grind it to blue dust in a mortar and drop it into a village well on the first full moon. Nobody in that village falls sick for years. You never tell them why.

events.text: An apothecary in a back street keeps a jar labelled AZURE DRAGON, and when you ask, opens it: blue-green powder, a pinch for a tael, for the heart. It is chalk and indigo. But the apothecary is honest about that, once asked, and then says: "My great-grandmother sold the real thing. She said it cried in the jar."

choices.text: Ask about the one who bought it

effects.log: "A sect alchemist," the apothecary says. "Who never slept again. She said that at the end the alchemist went east to apologise to a ridge, and the ridge was not there any more." The apothecary closes the jar. "I sell chalk now. Chalk does not cry."

choices.text: Buy a pinch of chalk anyway (1 tael)

effects.log: You put it in a little paper and carry it all your life, for no reason you can name. It is the cheapest thing you own and the one you would save from a fire.

events.text: A great old temple, and beside its main hall a small mossy pond the monks call the Nine Dragon Pond, though, they say, only one is left. When you kneel at the edge to wash your hands, the water bulges and a head comes up, blue-green, whiskered, with eyes as white as milk. It cannot see you. It turns toward you anyway, the way the blind turn toward a voice they have not heard in a thousand years.
events.arc: The Blind Dragon of the Temple

choices.text: Speak to it

effects.log: You say only "It is me," not knowing why. The milky eyes close. "I know," it says, in a voice like water under a floor. "I would know you blind. I am blind." It sounds, for a dragon, almost merry.

choices.text: Feed it rice from your palm

effects.log: It finds your palm by smell and eats the rice grain by grain, very carefully, as if it were a rite. The old monk watching from the hall drops his broom.

events.text: The temple of the blind dragon is under threat: a governor wants its pond filled in for a new hall. The abbot, who is very old, asks you to stand with the monks. "It swore to guard us," the abbot says, "the day the great monk boiled its pond with the word for fire. It has kept its word for a thousand years. Somebody should keep one to it."
events.arc: The Blind Dragon of the Temple

choices.text: Stand at the pond with the monks

ok.log: The governor's labourers come with baskets of earth and find you sitting on the edge of the pond. Then they find what is in the pond, rising behind you, blind and very large. They go home. The governor builds the hall somewhere else.

fail.log: There is a scuffle. You go into the pond. Something catches you and holds you up, very gently, until the labourers have run. The pond is not filled. (-15 health)

choices.text: Go to the governor with the temple's old records

ok.log: You read the governor the story of the boiled pond, the three dead dragons, the five that fled, the one that stayed. The governor is a careful official. The pond stays. A new hall is built facing it, with a window.

fail.log: The governor laughs at old stories. The labourers come. They do not get far: the pond boils, by itself, as it did once before, and they drop their baskets and run.

events.text: At the edge of a cliff above the temple of the blind dragon there is a red-stained rock the monks call Dragon Blood Rock, and in the valley beyond, the Five Dragon Valley. You have never been here. You stand on the cliff and feel, suddenly, three deaths and five flights and one staying, as if they were your own brothers and sisters.
events.arc: The Blind Dragon of the Temple

choices.text: Pray for the three who died

effects.log: You kneel at the red rock and say what you can. The wind goes over the cliff in three long breaths. Down at the temple, the blind dragon lifts its head from the pond and turns it toward the cliff, and keeps it there until you stand.

choices.text: Go down into the Five Dragon Valley

effects.log: Five streams come together in the valley, and on each, in the sun, something long and blue-green is lying very still. None of them looks at you. All of them know you are there. You walk through, carefully, as through a room of sleepers.

events.text: The palace pond under the great banquet pavilion is being drained to be cleaned, for the first time in two hundred years. You are among the crowd that has come to watch. At the bottom, in the black mud, the labourers find a bronze dragon the length of a man, green with age, its head turned up toward the pavilion. When they lift it out, every brazier in the palace gutters at once.
events.arc: The Bronze Dragon in the Pond

choices.text: Tell them to put it back at once

ok.log: Something in your voice makes the overseer obey without thinking. The bronze dragon goes back into the mud, head up. The braziers settle. That winter, when the kitchens catch fire, the flames go out on their own in a single breath.

fail.log: They take it to the treasury to be catalogued. That night the east wing burns. The next morning the overseer, ash on his face, quietly has it carried back and sunk where it was.

choices.text: Touch the bronze

effects.log: It is warm, which bronze out of cold mud should not be. Under your hand you feel two fires, and a third, and then a long cool lying-down in the dark under the water, for ever, so that nothing above would burn again. You take your hand away very slowly.

events.text: Fire again in the capital, a whole quarter of it, driven by a dry wind. It comes up to the palace walls and stops there as if at a line drawn in ink. From the wall, where the watchers have gathered, you see the pond under the banquet pavilion steaming, gently, the whole night through.
events.arc: The Bronze Dragon in the Pond

choices.text: Go down to the pond and keep it company

effects.log: You sit on the stone edge until dawn. Once, near the fourth watch, the water at the centre stirs, and something heavy and green turns over beneath it, like a guard shifting weight from one foot to the other.

choices.text: Lead the bucket lines in the burning quarter

effects.log: All night in the smoke, among people who do not have a bronze dragon in their pond. You save a street. In the morning you go to the palace pond, black with soot, and bow to it. (-8 health)

events.text: You come to a valley the old county records say has never once had a bad year: no drought, no flood, no plague, no locusts, for a thousand years. Nobody in it can say why. "Luck," they say, and shrug, and go on threshing. On the left of the valley a long gentle ridge curls round it like an arm round a sleeping child. Standing at its foot, you feel your own pulse slow to match something.
events.arc: The Valley That Never Has a Bad Year

choices.text: Stay a season in the valley

effects.log: Spring, summer, autumn. You help with the rice. The harvest is, of course, perfect. On the last evening you lie on the ridge and fall asleep, and wake with your hand on the ground and the clear sense that the ground had its hand on you.

choices.text: Tell the villagers the ridge is the reason

effects.log: They laugh, politely. "The ridge is a ridge," an old woman says. Then she adds, thoughtfully: "My grandmother used to leave rice at its foot. We stopped. Nothing changed." She goes on threshing. You think: that is what a good guardian is like.

events.text: A lord has bought the lucky valley and plans to quarry the left ridge for building stone. The surveyors have already marked the first cut. The villagers do not mind: it is only a ridge.
events.arc: The Valley That Never Has a Bad Year

choices.text: Buy the ridge from the lord yourself (200 taels)

effects.log: Two hundred taels for a ridge nobody wants. The lord thinks you are a fool. You walk the length of it the day the deed is signed, and under your feet, very faintly, it breathes, as it has for a thousand years, and as it will.

choices.text: Show the lord what is under the first cut

ok.log: You put your palm on the marked rock and push your qi down into it until it answers, and the whole ridge shivers like a horse's flank. The surveyors drop their tools. The lord quarries somewhere else, and does not say why.

fail.log: The ridge does not answer you. The first cut is made. That spring, for the first time in a thousand years, the valley floods. The lord stops quarrying. (-12 health)

choices.text: Let it be: a vein is not yours to keep twice

effects.log: You walk away. The quarrymen come with picks, and strike, and the picks bounce off the stone like straws. After a month they give up. The valley has its thousand and first good year.

events.text: A village between two ridges: on the left a long green one, on the right a crouching white-rocked one. The villagers call them Grandfather Dragon and Grandmother Tiger and put rice at both feet at the new year. Tonight, from the bridge in the middle of the village, you see two shapes in the dusk clouds over the two ridges, an azure one and a white one, both looking down at the village, and then, both at once, at you.
events.arc: The Village Between Dragon and Tiger

choices.text: Bow to the left, then to the right

effects.log: Left, then right, as a guest would. The clouds dissolve. That night you sleep in the village inn and dream of lying on a ridge in the sun with somebody large and white lying on the ridge opposite, and of neither of you needing to say anything for a thousand years.

choices.text: Ask the villagers if the two ever quarrel

effects.log: "Once a century," the innkeeper says comfortably. "About the rain. Then it rains on both sides at once and everybody gets wet." He laughs. "Nobody here remembers a bad year. We do not even have a word for it."

events.text: Bandits, a hundred of them, coming up the valley road toward the village between the two ridges. The village has no walls. The headman is calm. "Watch," he says, and goes on with his supper.
events.arc: The Village Between Dragon and Tiger

choices.text: Watch

effects.log: At the valley mouth the bandits stop. On their left, the green ridge has lifted its head. On their right, the white one has stood up. The bandits stand very still for a long time. Then they go home, the long way, and some of them become farmers.

choices.text: Go down to the valley mouth anyway, sword drawn

effects.log: You stand at the valley mouth alone, feeling brave, and then feel the two ridges on either side of you rise, and feel considerably less necessary. The bandits flee. The headman sends you a bowl of his supper, still warm, with a note: thank you for trying.

events.text: At a court you are visiting, a young royal of the ruling house stops in front of you in a corridor and stares. {npc} has sea-coloured eyes, and behind one ear, half hidden by the hair, a blue-green scale the size of a coin. "Every one of our line has one," {npc} says. "From the founder's grandmother, who was a dragon. You are looking at it as if you have seen it before."

choices.text: Say that you have, a long time ago

effects.log: {npc} touches the scale, slowly. "The genealogy says the dragon left because it was watched sleeping," {he} says. "Do you think the dragon forgave the archer?" You say yes so quickly, and so sure, that {npc} looks at you for a long time.

choices.text: Bow, as to a royal

effects.log: You bow. {npc} returns it, a fraction lower than a royal should. Neither of you knows why. Both of you, for a moment, smell the sea.

events.text: {npc}, of the dragon's line, has come to you in secret. A coup is coming: a minister with an army wants the throne, and the royal house will be cut down to the last child. "The genealogy says that when the line is in danger," {npc} says, "someone will come who remembers the sea. I think it is you."

choices.text: Defend the royal house

ok.log: Three nights of fighting in palace corridors. On the third, the minister's army breaks in the rain, and every one of the dragon's line is alive in the morning. {npc} finds you on the palace wall at dawn and touches your shoulder, and says nothing at all.

fail.log: There are too many swords in the corridors.
fail.deathCause: the coup against the Dragon's Line

choices.text: Smuggle the youngest children out to the coast

effects.log: Five children, a fishing boat, a night with no moon. Off the coast the sea lifts the boat gently and carries it, all night, faster than any wind, to an island no map shows. The line goes on, out there, waiting.

events.text: Fishing villages on the west coast tell a story: a dragon married an archer, and slept behind a closed door, and was watched, and went back into the sea through a well in the yard, and the well is still there. A child offers to show you, for a copper.

choices.text: Pay the copper and look into the well

effects.log: An ordinary old well in a ruined yard. You look down. The water is warm. It should not be. Far below, something turns over, the way a sleeper turns when someone they love comes into the room.

choices.text: Tell the child the end of the story

effects.log: "She forgave him," you say. The child frowns. "That is not how it ends." "It is how it ended," you say. The child thinks about this, and then charges the next traveller two coppers, for the new ending.

events.text: A village shaman is performing the rite of the five directions at the new year: five colours of cloth, five generals called, and for the east, the Blue Emperor, who is spring. The shaman spins east with a blue fan and stops dead, facing you. The bells go silent. "Oh," the shaman says, in an entirely different voice. "It is you. It is very strange to be called by yourself."

choices.text: Answer the voice

effects.log: "Hello," you say, feeling foolish. The voice laughs, and every plum tree in the village opens at once, in the snow, a month early. The shaman falls down and sleeps for a day. Spring, that year, comes to that valley first in all the country.

choices.text: Bow, and let the rite go on

effects.log: You bow to the shaman and to whatever is in the shaman. The voice says, "Polite. Good," and goes, and the rite carries on, west to the White Tiger, south to the Red Bird. But the east wind that night is warm.

events.text: A late frost has killed the blossom in three provinces, and the farmers are saying it will be a hungry year. You walk out into the black orchards at dawn and, without knowing why, breathe out toward the east as hard as you can.

choices.text: Breathe again, with all your qi

ok.log: The east wind comes back to you like an echo, warm, and goes over the orchards, and the black buds that were dead are green by noon. The farmers will tell it for generations. They will get the name wrong. You do not correct them.

fail.log: You breathe until you fall over. Nothing happens. Then, three days later, a second blossom, thin and late and enough. You are never sure. (-10 health)

choices.text: Help the farmers plant a second crop instead

effects.log: Millet and beans in the spaces where the fruit should be. It is not a good year. It is not a hungry one. In the autumn the dead orchards put out, all at once, out of season, one blossom each.

events.text: In the Upper Realm there is a palace in the east where it is always the first morning of spring. The gatekeeper does not ask your name. "The Emperor is out," {npc} says. "Being spring, somewhere. But the Emperor said that if you ever came, you were to be let in and given tea. The Emperor said you would know the way."

choices.text: Go in and sit on the empty throne for one breath

effects.log: One breath. In it you feel every spring there has ever been, all at once, rising in every world like sap. You get up before the second breath, which, the gatekeeper tells you afterwards, is the right number.

choices.text: Drink the tea and leave a note

effects.log: The tea tastes of the first rain on a dry field. Your note says only: the well, the first full moon. {npc} folds it carefully. "The Emperor will laugh," {he} says. "The Emperor does not laugh enough."

events.text: An empty village. Thirty houses, roofs fallen in, no one left; the last family went three generations ago, the magistrate's records say, "for no reason". Above it the left-hand ridge is grey and bare, and along its spine, black with age, nine iron stakes still stand in the rock. Your mouth fills with the taste of iron. Your heart hurts.

choices.text: Pull the stakes, one by one

ok.log: Nine days. Each one comes out dry and rusted and cold. When the ninth is out you lie on the ridge and wait, and nothing happens, for a long time. Then, at dawn, under your cheek, so faint you might have imagined it: one breath.

fail.log: Six come out. The last three will not move, rusted into the rock as if grown there. You leave them, for now, with your hands bleeding. (-15 health)

choices.text: Find out who drove them

effects.log: The magistrate's archive has it, in a hand that shakes: a hall with no sign on its gate, a rival house's payment, a date. The hall is still there. It is very prosperous. You copy the record out carefully.

events.text: You come back to the empty village under the dead ridge. Someone has planted a pine sapling where the ninth stake was. It is green. There is a family camped in the ruins of the headman's house, a man and two children, who heard that the valley was cursed and could not afford anywhere that was not.

choices.text: Help them rebuild

effects.log: A season of roof timbers and mud walls. In the autumn their little field gives a harvest, not a good one, an ordinary one, which for that valley is a miracle. The children call the ridge Grandfather and leave it rice.

choices.text: Tell them the story of the ridge

effects.log: You tell them about the stakes and the hall and the three generations. The man listens and then says: "Then it needs neighbours more than we do." They stay. The next spring two more families come.

events.text: The hall with no sign on its gate: still here, still prosperous, still full of maps of other people's valleys pinned with iron nails. Its current master, {npc}, receives you courteously. "We cut a famous vein once," {npc} says. "A dragon, they said. It bled for a hundred years. Our founder considered it the masterwork of the art. Why do you ask?"

choices.text: Challenge {npc} to a duel for the maps

ok.log: It is a long fight in a courtyard full of iron. When it is over the maps burn in the brazier, all of them, and a hundred valleys you will never see breathe easier. {npc} watches the smoke and says nothing.

fail.log: {npc} is very good, with something of iron in every blow. You leave over the wall. But you leave knowing the hall's defences, and that is a start. (-25 health)

choices.text: Tell {npc} who you were

effects.log: You tell {npc} plainly. {npc} laughs, and then stops laughing, because you are not. That night, you hear later, the master of the hall sat alone with the founder's tablet until dawn. The next year the hall takes no new commissions.

events.text: In the eastern mountains there is a ridge of bare grey stone that is exactly the shape of a dragon lying face down, with its head on its paws. The locals call it the Fallen One and do not build near it, and do not climb it, and cannot say why. You climb it. At the top, sitting on its brow, you feel it remember flying too high, and the long, long fall, and every year since.

choices.text: Sit with it through the night

effects.log: All night, under the seven stars of the east. Toward dawn you feel, very faintly, the stone under you shift, the way a person shifts when somebody finally sits beside them. You come down with the oldest kind of sorrow settled in you, and it is not heavy, only deep.

choices.text: Tell it, aloud, that pride is forgiven

ok.log: You say it to the stars and the stone. Nothing moves. But in the spring the locals report, frightened, that moss has grown on the Fallen One for the first time, green all along its back, as if it had decided to stop being stone.

fail.log: The words sound small up there. Pride is not forgiven by being told so. You come down humbler yourself, which, you think later, is perhaps what it wanted.

events.text: Your sect, or your town, or your family, wants to raise a great statue of you in the square, because of what you have done. The plans are drawn up. The statue is very tall. Every time you look at the plans, you feel the cold of grey stone and a long fall.

choices.text: Forbid the statue

effects.log: They are disappointed and do not understand. You ask them to dig a well instead. They do, grudgingly. It is the best well in the province, and nobody remembers who asked for it, which is exactly right.

choices.text: Allow it, but small, and facing east

effects.log: A statue the height of a child, facing the sunrise, bowing a little. People laugh at first. Then they start leaving rice at its feet, the way they do for small gods.

choices.text: Let them build it tall

effects.log: It is magnificent. It is the tallest thing in the province. In its third winter, on a still night, it falls on its face in the square, and nobody can find any reason why.

events.text: The Fallen One, the ridge of grey stone you once sat on: word has come that it is green now from end to end, pines on its back, a spring at its head. And that on the last spring equinox, the locals swear, it lifted its head an inch off its paws, and looked at the eastern sky, and put it down again, content.

choices.text: Go and see

effects.log: It is green. A spring comes out of its brow and runs down past where its eye would be, like a tear that has learned to be a stream. You sit on its head again. This time it feels like sitting on an old friend.

choices.text: Stay where you are, and look east at the equinox

effects.log: At dawn on the equinox you face east from wherever you are. You do not see anything. You feel something very far off lift its head an inch, and you lift yours.

events.text: First full moon. Everyone is racing to the well at first cockcrow. You are not running. You are walking, slowly, because you already know what is at the bottom: you were it, once, and you went back to it, and something in you has been waiting all your life to see whether it is there again.

choices.text: Look down

effects.log: Under the black water, on the stones: an egg, blue-green, lit from inside. It turns toward you. You have the dizzying sense of looking into a mirror from the wrong side. It knows you. It is you. It is, also, entirely its own, and it is beginning again.

choices.text: Draw the first water and carry it home, as you were carried

ok.log: You are first, by a stride. The bucket is heavy. You carry the jar home on your head with both hands, the way someone once carried you, and set it down in the kitchen, and sit beside it until noon, crying, without knowing exactly why.

fail.log: A child beats you to it, and floats the straw, and carries the jar home on her head, staggering, delighted. You watch her go. You feel, absurdly, that you are in good hands.

events.text: A drought, and the village children are being put in blue robes to catch lizards for the rain rite. One of them is standing at the door of a house you know, looking at a water jar in its kitchen, the way you once looked at a child in blue from the bottom of a jar.

choices.text: Take the child fishing instead

effects.log: You spend the whole day on the river with the child and catch nothing, and talk about everything, and when you bring the child home at dusk the lizard rite is over and the jar in that kitchen is still full, and quietly, at the bottom, glowing.

choices.text: Go into the kitchen and sit by the jar

effects.log: You sit by it with your back to the door like a guard. Nobody comes in. At sunset the water in the jar ripples, once, a ring from the middle out, the way water answers someone it has been waiting for.

events.text: Very old now, you go down to the well on the first full moon one last time. You are not first. You are last. When everyone has drawn and gone, you lean on the rim and look down, and something long and blue, dog-sized, comes up through the water and puts its chin on the surface, and looks at you.

choices.text: Say goodbye

effects.log: "See you," you say, which is not goodbye at all. It blows a single bubble, which bursts and smells of spring. You walk home very slowly, and very happy, and do not need to look back.

choices.text: Ask it whether it will do better this time

effects.log: It considers you for a long time with its old new eyes. Then it does the most humble thing a dragon can do: it shrugs. You laugh so hard you have to sit down on the rim.

events.text: The tenth day of the fifth month. All your life it has rained on this day, every year, wherever you were, even in a desert once, out of a clear sky. People who know you have stopped being surprised. This year, standing in the rain in a strange town, an old scholar beside you says: "The King's Rain. A dragon keeps a dead king's word. Did you know it follows some people?"

choices.text: Say you knew

effects.log: The scholar nods as if that settled something, and you stand together in the warm rain, two strangers, and neither of you puts up a hat.

choices.text: Ask the scholar who it follows

effects.log: "Those who carried the promise," the scholar says. "Or who were it. The stories disagree." The rain gets heavier, warm as bathwater. "I think it is only being polite. It remembers who it owes."

events.text: A dying ruler, in a dry year, has heard of you: the person it always rains on, on the tenth day of the fifth month. {npc} wants you to stand in the palace courtyard on that day, so that the rain will fall on the capital.

choices.text: Go to the capital for the day

effects.log: You stand in the palace courtyard at noon on the tenth day of the fifth month. It rains, warm and heavy, on the whole capital and the fields around it. {npc} dies a month later with the rice green to the horizon.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the rain is not yours to bring

effects.log: You explain, as kindly as you can, that a promise kept is not a tool. {npc} is angry, and then thoughtful. On the tenth day of the fifth month it rains on the capital anyway, without you, because some promises are bigger than the person who keeps them.

events.text: A young tomb painter, painting the guardian of the east on a lord's burial chamber, has never seen a dragon and paints it with eyes closed, "from memory, the way everyone does". You hold the lamp. When the eye is done, you recognise it. It is the look you give yourself in a basin of water in the morning.

choices.text: Tell the painter it is a good likeness

effects.log: The painter laughs, thinking you are joking. You are not. All your life after that, when you pass the east wall of any old shrine, the painted dragon seems to give you a small, private nod.

choices.text: Ask the painter who taught that face

effects.log: "Nobody," the painter says. "Every painter just knows it. Painters have always known it. Since the Guardian took the east wall of the sky." The painter shrugs. "It is in the hand."

events.text: On a clear spring night you look up at the seven stars of the eastern sky, Horn to Winnowing Basket, and for the first time in this life they are not stars: they are a body, long and coiled, and in the place of the red Heart star, an eye, and the eye is looking down, as it has every night, at you and everyone else.

choices.text: Look back up for as long as it looks down

effects.log: Until dawn. It does not blink. You do, eventually. When the sun comes up you find you are no longer afraid of anything that can happen in one life.

choices.text: Wave

effects.log: You feel ridiculous. Somewhere very high up, the Heart star flickers, red and gold, twice. You go to bed grinning like a child.

events.text: Every autumn, all your life, you have felt a pull: to go down into the dark and not come up again until spring. This autumn, by a still black lake in the mist, the pull is so strong you sit down on the bank. Far below the surface, something coiled is sleeping. It has been sleeping for a very long time. It decided once not to rise.
events.arc: The Lake That Does Not Wake

choices.text: Call down to it to wake

effects.log: You call. Nothing wakes. But the surface ripples, once, in a slow ring, as if something very deep had turned over and murmured, "Not yet." You find you are glad of it.

choices.text: Sit by it through the autumn, and rest

effects.log: You stay until the first snow, doing nothing at all, for the first time in your life. When you get up, everything that has been pressing on you for years has been rinsed off, as if by deep water. In the spring you rise, and get on with it.
